Q. What is McLeod syndrome and McLeod phenotype?

·       Kx blood group

·       XK gene

·       XK protein reduced

·       Kx antigen lack on RBC membrane (as well as Km antigen)

·       Weakened expression of Kell system antigens

·       X-linked, almost exclusive in male

·       Acanthocytosis, shortened RBC survival, late onset neuromuscular defects, increased CK

·       McLeod with CGD -> produce anti-Km and anti-Kx -> only compatible with McLeod RBC

·       McLeod without CGD -> produce anti-Km -> compatible with McLeod and K0 RBC

Q. What is Rh-null phenotype?

·       RHAG gene mutation

·       Autosomal recessive

·       RHAG protein absent

·       RBC leak cations (K+, Na+)

·       Chronic hemolytic anemia with stomatocytosis

·       Absence of all Rh antigens, weakly react with anti-Rh29

·       Sequencing of RHAG, RHD, RHCE genes

·       Increased RBC osmotic fragility due to membrane defects

·       Rh-null can develop antibody against Rh antigens

·       Must receive Rh-null blood

G

Rh

G is present on any red cell that carries either the D or C antigen (or both). This means that G is only absent when a person’s red cells lack both D and C.

The vast majority of G-negative people who could make anti-G are D-negative with the rr genotype.

Anti-G is seen is in a D-negative patient who has never been knowingly exposed to Rh-positive blood, yet presents with an antibody that looks like a combination of both anti-D and anti-C (sometimes called “anti-CD”)

If a D-negative mom has anti-G, she does still need Rh prophylaxis in the form of Rh Immune Globulin. If, instead, she has anti-D plus anti-C, Rh prophylaxis is not indicated, since she is already immunized.

Antibody

Type

Reactivity

Clinical Significance

Transfusion Recommendations

HDFN Risk

ABO System

Naturally occurring IgM antibodies (anti-A, anti-B); some IgG forms may exist.

Strongly reactive at 37°C; causes immediate hemolysis in incompatible transfusions.

Major cause of acute hemolytic transfusion reactions (HTRs); most severe in ABO-incompatible transfusions.

Only ABO-compatible blood must be transfused.

Rarely causes HDFN; IgG forms may cause mild to moderate HDFN.

Rh (D) Antibody

IgG; produced after exposure (e.g., pregnancy, transfusion).

Reactive at 37°C and the antiglobulin phase.

Most significant cause of HDFN; can cause severe anemia, hydrops fetalis, and stillbirth.

Rh-negative individuals must receive Rh-negative blood. Rh-negative pregnant individuals with anti-D require monitoring.

High risk of severe HDFN if the fetus is Rh-positive. Preventable with Rh immunoglobulin (RhIg) administration to Rh-negative mothers.

Lewis System

IgM; naturally occurring; primarily in Le(a–b–) individuals.

Cold-reactive; anti-Lea may react at 37°C; anti-Leb is weaker.

Rarely cause HTRs. Do not cause HDFN as they don't cross the placenta.

Crossmatch-compatible units are generally sufficient.

Not implicated in HDFN.

P1 Antibody

Naturally occurring IgM in P1– individuals.

Cold-reactive, typically at 4°C; rare cases may react at 37°C.

Usually clinically insignificant unless reacting at 37°C. Rare cause of HTRs.

Crossmatch-compatible units at 37°C; antigen typing generally not required.

Not implicated in HDFN.

Anti-I

IgM; common autoantibody, found in virtually all individuals.

Cold-reactive at 4°C; stronger forms may bind complement.

Usually benign. Pathogenic forms may cause cold agglutinin disease or hemolytic anemia.

Manage cold-reactive antibodies during pretransfusion testing; avoid room temperature incubation.

Not implicated in HDFN as anti-I is IgM and poorly expressed on infant RBCs.

Anti-i

Rare IgM autoantibody; reacts strongly with cord RBCs.

Cold-reactive, mainly with i-positive cells (cord RBCs).

Typically benign. Occasionally associated with infections or lymphoproliferative disorders. Rarely contributes to hemolysis.

Antigen-negative units are rarely required due to weak expression of i antigen.

Rarely associated with HDFN; IgG forms may cause mild HDFN.

Anti-M

Naturally occurring; mostly IgM; 50-80% may have an IgG component.

Cold-reactive, typically below 37°C; does not bind complement.

Usually clinically insignificant unless reactive at 37°C. Rare cause of HTRs or HDFN.

Crossmatch-compatible units; M antigen typing not necessary unless reactive at 37°C.

Rarely implicated in HDFN.

Anti-N

Mostly IgM; rarely IgG.

Cold-reactive; demonstrates dosage effect.

Not significant unless reactive at 37°C. Rare cases associated with dialysis (anti-Nf).

IAT-compatible blood for transfusion.

Rarely implicated in HDFN.

Anti-S / Anti-s

Predominantly IgG.

Reactive at 37°C and the antiglobulin phase; may show dosage effect.

Clinically significant; cause severe HTRs and HDFN.

Antigen-negative, crossmatch-compatible units must be selected.

Significant risk of HDFN.

Anti-K

IgG; produced in response to exposure (e.g., pregnancy or transfusion).

Reacts at 37°C; persists for years.

Common cause of severe HTRs and HDFN; suppresses fetal erythropoiesis leading to fetal anemia.

Antigen-negative blood must be selected. Close fetal monitoring if present in pregnant individuals.

Severe risk of HDFN; can cause stillbirth even at low antibody titers.

Anti-Fya / Anti-Fyb

IgG; produced after immunization.

Reactive at 37°C and the antiglobulin phase.

Causes immediate and delayed HTRs; implicated in HDFN.

Antigen-negative, crossmatch-compatible units must be selected.

Both have the potential to cause HDFN.

Anti-Jka / Anti-Jkb

IgG; can be difficult to detect.

Reactive at 37°C; often missed in testing but may cause hemolysis.

Dangerous antibodies; common cause of delayed HTRs. Rarely causes HDFN.

Antigen-negative blood must be selected.

Rarely implicated in severe HDFN.

o   Rh

  • Complement Binding: Some antibodies (e.g., anti-Kidd, anti-I) bind complement, which may enhance hemolysis.
  • Delayed Detection: Kidd antibodies often drop to undetectable levels quickly, leading to delayed hemolytic reactions.

Low incidence Ag and Ab

G antigen & antibody

1. The G Antigen

  • Present whenever D and/or C antigen is present on red blood cells.
  • Absent only when both D and C are absent (e.g., in most D-negative individuals with rr genotype).
  • Biochemically linked to a serine residue common to D and C antigens.

2. Anti-G Antibody

  • Formed by D-negative, G-negative (rr) individuals after exposure to G-positive blood (pregnancy or transfusion).
  • Appears like a combination of anti-D and anti-C, leading to potential misidentification.
  • Key distinction: It reacts with both D+ and C+ RBCs, but it's a single antibody, not two separate ones.

3. Clinical Relevance

  • Transfusion:
    • No major impact—D-negative patients with anti-G receive D-negative blood, same as if they had anti-D + anti-C.
  • Pregnancy & RhIG Administration:
    • Critical to differentiate anti-G from anti-D in pregnant women.
    • If true anti-D is absent, RhIG is still needed to prevent future anti-D formation.
    • If anti-D is already present, RhIG is not needed.

4. Laboratory Testing & Differentiation

  • G-Differentiation (Classic method):
    • Adsorption with D+ C- cells removes anti-D & anti-G, leaving anti-C in serum.
    • A second adsorption with D- G+ cells isolates anti-G.
  • D-Differentiation (Simplified method):
    • Determines if anti-D is truly present after adsorption.
    • If anti-D is absent, assume anti-G and give RhIG.
    • If anti-D is present, RhIG is not needed.

U antigen

What is the U antigen?

The U antigen is a ‘high incidence’ antigen, present on the red cells of 99% of Black and virtually 100% of Caucasian people.

Glycophorin B forms the stem for antigens S and s.

U-negative individuals have absent or altered gylcophorin B.

If you have U, you may or may not have S or s.

If you don’t have U, you can’t have S or s, and could form Anti-U alloantibodies.

Anti-U can target the U antigen regardless of whether S or s is present.

example scenario

 

Qu. A woman with sickle cell anaemia is found to have an Anti-U alloantibody during her pregnancy booking bloods. She does not currently require blood. Later in the pregnancy she is found to have placenta praevia. What does this mean for the patient and what will you do?

 

Mother

Antenatal

  • Monitor titre (serial dilution IAT)
  • USS for MCA dopplers, amniotic fluid volume
  • Refer fetomaternal unit, MDT approach

Delivery

  • Planned C-section
  • Pre-op anaemia Mx
  • Cell salvage

Sourcing blood:

  • 1st choice – Is there any fresh U neg in stock?
  • 2nd choice - Blood from a directed donor – fresh, longer shelf-life, better quality.
  • 3rd choice – Frozen blood bank

 

Would you use relatives as directed donors?

Risk is the increased pressure to lie on the donor safety check forms.

Would need irradiating up to 2nd degree relatives. 

 

Baby

At risk of HDFN. (Anti-U can target U antigen even buried beneath S or s.)

  • Cord blood at birth – DAT (—> elution if positive), Group, FBC, Bilirubin
  • Monitor for jaundice
  • Will need U neg blood at birth if transfused due to maternal antibody

Q. How do you do ABO typing on a gel card?

●      Note difference in RBC concentration:

○      3-5% RBC solution for → tube testing

○      0.8% RBC solution for → gel cards

 

●      1) Forward grouping

○      You just add your patients 0.8% red cell suspension

○      Because the anti-A and B are already in the gel card matrix (don’t need to manually add reagent antibodies as you do in tube testing)

●      2) Reverse

○      You add reagent RBCs and your patient plasma/serum (in that order!)

●      3) Centrifuge

●      4) Read

Q. What collection tube preservative do we use for blood transfusion testing?

●      EDTA blood specimen (lavender stopper) 6 mL

●      Transport – RT

●      Storage – 2-6 degrees Celsius for 96 hours

Q. Causes of additional reactivity on forward grouping?

●      Acquired antigens (acquired B in group A patient)

●      B(A) phenotype (B with weak A in forward, anti-A only in reverse)

●      Polyagglutinable red cells

●      Transfusion (mixed field)

●      BMT

●      Non-specific agglutination (eg. silica glass tubes, wharton's jelly)

●      Sensitized red cells (covered in antibody)

Q. Causes of decreased reactivity on forward grouping? (Group 2 discrepancy, weakened antigen expression)

●      Antigen altered by disease (leukemia with chromosome 9 abnormalities, lymphomas)

●      Large volume of O transfusion

●      Chimera

●      Weak subgroup of A or B (reacts poorly with anti-A or -B)

●      Neonate with poor ABO expression

●      Pancreatic Ca/ Biliary (secrete type 1 chains!)

Q. Causes of additional reactivity on reverse typing?(unexpected antibody)

●      Alloantibody with reactivity on immediate spin (ex. IgM)

●      Autoantibody (IgM class)

●      Passive transfer of antibody due to transfusion of product (IVIG, out of group PLTs or plasma)

●      Transfusion and resultant passive alloimmunization

●      Rouleaux (address with saline replacement)

●      Subgroup A (eg A2 with anti-A1)

Q. Causes of decreased reactivity on reverse grouping? (Group 1 discrepancy, reduced antibody production)

●      Newborns or elderly

●      Hypogammaglobulinemia (leukemia, lymphoma, immunosuppressive drugs)

●      Agammaglobulinemia (congenital immunodeficiency)

●      BMT

●      Chimera (either reduced antigen expression or antibody production)

●      Apheresis (IgM antibodies removed in exchange transfusion)

●      Old reagent: deterioration of antigen on reagent RBCs with storage

●      ? large volume group AB plasma

Q. How does saline replacement resolve ABO discrepancy?

●      Removes the effect of rouleaux causing increased reactivity in the reverse group

●      Removes unwanted reactivity

Q. What are methods to increase reactivity when there is decreased reactivity in reverse grouping?

●      Incubate at room temperature for 15-30 minutes (longer incubation)

●      Increase serum ratio

●      Incubate at colder temp - can cool to 4 degrees → but must run group O control and AC when doing this to ensure you aren't reacting against something else.

Q. Technical errors causing ABO discrepancy?

●      Preanalytical:

○      Incorrect or inadequate identification of blood specimens, test tubes, or slides.

○      A mix-up in samples

○      Clerical errors

●      Analytical:

○      Failure to add reagents

○      Failure to add sample

○      Failure to follow manufacturer's instructions

○      Cell suspension too heavy or too light

■      3-5% RBC suspension for tube, 0.8% suspension for gel card - this is estimated visually

○      Over centrifugation or under centrifugation

○      Contaminated reagents, old or expired reagents

○      Warming during centrifugation

●      Postanalytical:

○      Missed observations of hemolysis

○      Interpretation error (subjective interpretation by tech)

○      Incorrect recording of results

Q. In what 3 circumstances is the ABO typing recorded as undetermined?

●      1) When there is an unresolved ABO/Rh discrepancy

●      2) When the pt is a bone marrow transplant recipient with an ABO mismatched donor

●      3) When the patient is within 6 months of having received a liver transplant with an ABO mismatched donor

Q. What is a typical policy on switching blood type after transplant (4 criteria)?

1.     Blood type has to match donor

2.     No mixed fields allowed

3.     DAT has to be negative

4.     No evidence of relapse

5.     Transfusion independent (? 3 months to 1 year)

Note: reverse group may never match the donor

 

Q. When can we stop irradiation for SCT patients?

●      No evidence of ongoing GVHD

●      Off immunosuppressants

Q. What is polyagglutination?

●      Non-specific agglutination that is most commonly caused by bacterial infections where bacterial enzymes strip off, or change, antigens causing exposure of “cryptantigens” → This referred to as “T activation” → the most common type of polyagglutination

●      People normally have naturally occurring IgM that will react against these cryptantigens.

●      Acquired polyagglutination is transient

Q. What are the 2 types of polyagglutination

●      “T activation” or polyagglutination

●      “Tn activation” or polyagglutination

Q. What is T activation?

●      1 of 2 types of polyagglutination

●      Caused by the removal of portions of glycophorin A and B chains on red cells which exposes → cryptantigens.

●      Usually occurs in children.

Q. What 4 pathogens have been known to cause T activation?

●      Streptococcus pneumoniae

●      Clostridium perfringens

●      Vibrio cholerae

●      Influenza Virus

●      Mnemonic “VICS”

Q. Is T-activation clinically significant and what blood product should theoretically be avoided?

●      Reports of hemolysis → with plasma transfusions exist.

●      Theoretically, plasma products will contain the naturally occurring IgM that will react against these cryptantigens possibly exacerbating the hemolysis

Q. What is Tn polyagglutination?

●      Caused by → mutations on X chromosome that results in abnormal synthesis of glycophorin A and B

Q. What is the B(A) phenotype mechanism and typing pattern?

●      Chimeric enzyme → making both B and A antigens

●      Forward typing → types like B (strong) with A (weak)

●      Reverse typing → will type like group B with strong anti-A

●      B(A) phenotype individuals have normal B antigen and B gene transfers a small amount of A sugar to the H antigen -> small amount of A antigen.

●      Some highly potent monoclonal anti-A reagents are capable of agglutinating B(A) RBCs, which therefore usually results in a discrepancy between RBC and plasma ABO grouping (unexpected weak forward reaction with anti-A)

●      Similar to acquired B. Resolution is test with another anti-A reagent from another manufacturer.

Q. What is acquired B phenotype?

●      Gram negative enteric organisms (ie. through colon cancer or infection)

●      Acetyl group is removed by bacterial enzymes

○      Deacetylates the A antigen N-Acetyl-D-galactosamine is converted to Galactosamine

○      Some reagents will recognize this as the normal B (galactose) in the forward group only

○      Forward Group: Normal A, Weak B; 

○      Reverse = Anti B (strong)

3.Subgroups

a.Bombay phenotype

(also known as hh phenotype)(Oh) is a rare blood group in which individuals lack the H antigen, which is the precursor for the A and B antigens found in the more common ABO blood groups. As a result, Bombay blood group individuals do not express A, B, or even H antigens on the surface of their red blood cells, even if their genotype suggests they should belong to the A, B, or AB blood groups.

ISBT system symbol

H

Bombay (Oh)

 

Q: What is the Bombay (Oh) phenotype?

·       Rare blood type with no H, A, or B antigens on red blood cells or in secretions.

 

Q: What causes the Bombay phenotype?

·       Mutations in both FUT1 (H gene) and FUT2 (secretor gene).

 

Q: Why can't Bombay individuals express A or B antigens?

·       Lack of H antigen, which is a precursor for A and B antigen formation.

 

Q: What antibodies are present in Bombay individuals?

·       Anti-H, anti-A, and anti-B antibodies.

 

Q: How do Bombay individuals typically type in routine blood tests?

·       Initially type as group O.

 

Q: How is the Bombay phenotype confirmed?

·       By testing for anti-H antibodies and absence of H antigen on red cells.

 

Q: What kind of blood can Bombay individuals receive?

·       Only from other Bombay phenotype donors.

 

Q: How does FUT1 differ from FUT2 in antigen formation?

·       FUT1 makes H antigen on red cells; FUT2 makes it in secretions.

 

Q: Why do Bombay individuals have difficulty with blood transfusions?

·       Their anti-H antibodies react with all regular ABO blood types.

 

Q. What lectin is used to identify H antigen?

·       Ulex europaeus agglutinin I (UEA I)

 

Q: What is the role of Ulex europaeus lectin in testing Bombay phenotype?

·       It binds to H antigen, helping confirm absence of H on red cells.

 

Summary:

  • Genotype: hh (lacks H antigen).
  • Antigens: No A, B, or H antigens on red blood cells.
  • Blood type: Appears as type O but reacts to all common blood types due to anti-H antibodies.
  • Transfusion: Can only receive blood from another Bombay phenotype donor.

 

b.Para-Bombay phenotype

Q: What is the Para-Bombay phenotype?

·       A rare blood type where individuals lack detectable H antigen on red cells but have weak A, B, or H antigens.

 

Q: What causes the Para-Bombay phenotype?

·       Nonfunctional FUT1 gene and at least one functional FUT2 (secretor gene).

 

Q: How is Para-Bombay different from Bombay?

·       Para-Bombay individuals can secrete ABH antigens in body fluids and have weak antigen expression on red cells.

 

Q: What antigens are present on Para-Bombay red cells?

·       Small amounts of H, A, and/or B antigens, adsorbed from plasma.

 

Q: Do Para-Bombay individuals produce anti-H antibodies?

·       Yes, but the anti-H antibodies are typically weaker than in Bombay individuals.

 

Q: How do Para-Bombay red cells react in laboratory testing?

·       Weak or no reaction with anti-H lectin, anti-A, or anti-B reagents.

 

Q: Can Para-Bombay individuals be secretors?

·       Yes, they can secrete ABH antigens in body fluids if they have a functional FUT2 gene.

 

Q: Can Para-Bombay occur in nonsecretors?

·       Yes, but in these cases, they have weak FUT1 activity and small amounts of H antigen on red cells.

 

Q: How does ABO inheritance affect Para-Bombay?

·       If A or B genes are inherited, weak A (Ah) or B (Bh) antigen may be expressed.

 

Q: How is Para-Bombay detected?

·       Through weak antigen reactions in blood testing, adsorption, and elution tests.

c.Secretor

Q: What is the difference between a secretor and a non-secretor?

·       Secretors have water-soluble ABH antigens in their body fluids (such as saliva, semen, and urine), while non-secretors do not.

·       However, both secretors and non-secretors have alcohol-soluble antigens on their red blood cells and tissues.

 

Q: What controls the secretion of ABH antigens in body fluids?

·       The secretion of ABH antigens in body fluids is controlled by the Se gene. Individuals with at least one functioning Se gene (SeSe or Sese) are secretors, while those with two non-functional alleles (sese) are non-secretors.

 

Q: Do secretors and non-secretors differ in the presence of ABH antigens on red blood cells?

·       No, both secretors and non-secretors have ABH antigens on their red blood cells. The difference is that secretors also have these antigens in their body fluids, while non-secretors do not.

 

Q: What happens in individuals with the Bombay phenotype (Oh)?

·       Individuals with the Bombay phenotype (hh genotype) do not produce A, B, or H antigens on their red blood cells, even if they possess ABO genes. They also do not secrete these antigens in their body fluids, regardless of whether they have the Se gene.

 

Q: How does the Se gene relate to the ABO and H genes?

·       The Se gene independently controls the secretion of ABH antigens in body fluids but does not affect the formation of A, B, or H antigens on red blood cells. The ABO and H genes determine the types of antigens on the red blood cells.

 

Q: Can a non-secretor have A, B, or H antigens on their red blood cells?

·       Yes, a non-secretor can have A, B, or H antigens on their red blood cells, but they will not secrete these antigens in their body fluids.

 

Q: What genotype results in a person being a non-secretor?

·       Individuals who are homozygous for the non-functional allele of the Se gene (genotype sese) are non-secretors.

 

Q: Why do Bombay phenotype individuals not secrete A, B, or H substances?

·       Bombay phenotype individuals (hh genotype) lack the H antigen, which is necessary for the formation of A and B antigens. As a result, they do not secrete A, B, or H substances, even if they have the Se gene.

 

d.Transfusion practice in Bombay/para-bombay phenotype

Q: What is alloanti-H in Bombay individuals?

·       A clinically significant antibody, predominantly IgM, that can cause hemolysis and acute transfusion reactions.

 

Q: How does alloanti-H behave in Bombay individuals?

·       Reacts with all red cells except Bombay cells and can cause complement activation and intravascular hemolysis.

 

Q: Is alloanti-H in Para-Bombay individuals clinically significant?

·       Yes, but it generally has lower titers and may be less likely to cause direct lysis, especially in secretors.

 

Q: What is autoanti-H?

·       Autoantibodies against H antigen, often seen in A1 individuals, usually of IgM type, reactive at room temperature.

 

Q: Are autoanti-H and autoanti-HI clinically significant?

·       Generally not. They usually don't affect transfusions, but rare cases can cause hemolysis.

 

Q: What should be done for Bombay patients needing transfusion?

·       They should receive H-negative (Bombay) red cells to avoid reactions.

 

Q: Is special care needed for Para-Bombay secretor patients during transfusion?

·       Not typically, but anti-H should be evaluated case by case, especially in nonsecretors.

 

Q: Can autoanti-HI cause transfusion reactions?

·       Rarely, it can cause hemolysis in patients with potent anti-HI after group O transfusion.

 

Q: What is the preferred transfusion for patients with high-titer autoanti-HI?

·       Transfuse group-specific red cells (A1, B, or AB) to avoid hemolysis.

 

Q: What is the isotype of most alloanti-H and autoanti-H antibodies?

·       Predominantly IgM.

 

e.A subtypes

Q. What is the agglutination pattern seen with most A subtypes?

●         Weak mixed field pattern → except Ael and Ax

 

 

Q. What causes A2?

●      Deletion late in the A transferase gene causing frameshift mutation, an additional 21 amino acids translated and a 5-10x decrease in enzyme activity.

Q. What is the clinical significance of A2?

●      Usually not clinically significant

●      Approximately 8-10% of A2 and 25% of A2B form Anti-A1 → which is clinically insignificant unless reactive at 37 degrees

Q. What percent of A blood group will be A2?

●      A1 80%

●      A2 20%

Q. What can be used to differentiate A1 and A2 serologically?

●      Only A1 cells are agglutinated by Dolichos biflorus lectin allowing differentiation from A2

●      Quantitative difference (A1 has 4x more epitopes) appears to be the method on which this works.

Q. What is a serologic feature of Ax?

●      Red cell phenotype agglutinated by only anti-A,B

Q. Ael agglutination pattern?

●      No agglutination.

●      Can only be demonstrated by adsorption elution studies

Q. What 2 B subgroups can only be demonstrated by adsorption/elution?

●      Bel and Bm

●      Think → “el” for elution in the case of both Ael and Bel subgroups

Q. What 2 B subgroups can have anti-B in their serum?

●      Bel and Bx

 

Rh testing

The purpose of blending monoclonal anti-D and polyclonal anti-D for use in an anti-D reagent is to...

·       provide room temperature agglutination (monoclonal)

·       enhance sensitivity for detection of weak D phenotype (polyclonal)

Weak D and Partial D

General Transfusion Recommendations:

  1. ABO and RhD Typing:
    • Perform ABO grouping and RhD typing as standard pre-transfusion tests.
    • For patients with weak or variable D antigen expression, consider further investigation using serologic weak D tests or molecular genotyping.
  1. Weak D and Partial D Management:
    • Weak D (Types 1, 2, 3):
      • These individuals are not at risk for forming anti-D antibodies.
      • Treat as RhD positive for transfusion and Rh immune globulin (RhIG) administration.
    • Partial D:
      • These individuals may form anti-D antibodies when exposed to normal D antigen.
      • Treat as RhD negative, especially for transfusion and pregnancy management.
  1. Rh Immune Globulin Use:
    • Administer RhIG to RhD-negative pregnant women or those at risk of alloimmunization.
    • Avoid unnecessary RhIG administration to patients with weak D Types 1, 2, and 3.
  1. Blood Conservation:
    • Reserve RhD-negative blood for patients who are truly RhD-negative or partial D to preserve the limited RhD-negative inventory.
  1. Genotyping Recommendations:
    • Consider RhD genotyping in:
      • Pregnant women with discrepant D typing results.
      • Patients with serologic weak D results.
      • Chronically transfused individuals to minimize unnecessary RhD-negative transfusions.

 

4.DAT

·       Antiglobulin Test (Coombs Test):
A laboratory test used to detect antibodies or complement components bound to red blood cells (RBCs), either in vivo (direct antiglobulin test) or in vitro (indirect antiglobulin test). It is essential for diagnosing immune-mediated hemolysis and ensuring transfusion compatibility.

·       Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT):
A test that detects antibodies (IgG) or complement (C3) attached to RBCs in vivo. Commonly used to diagnose conditions like autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN), and transfusion reactions.

·       Indirect Antiglobulin Test (IAT):
A test that identifies antibodies present in a patient’s serum that can bind to RBC antigens in vitro. It is used for antibody screening, crossmatching, and identifying specific alloantibodies.

 

 

What does a DAT detect?

 

●      In vivo sensitized RBCs (ab bound of RBC surface in vivo)

 

Q. What antibodies are coating the patients RBCs?

●       

Note: 3-5% RBC suspension for tube testing; 0.8% suspension for gel cards

 

Q. How is a DAT performed using a gel technique?

●      You take the patients red cells and suspend in a MTS diluent.

●      Bring the reagents to room temperature (18-25C).

●      Open a gel card and put the 0.8% red cell suspension into the gel card

●      Reagent ab’s are contained within the gel matrix of the columns in the card

●      Centrifuge at 895 +/-25 rpm for 10 minutes and read.

Q. What is a monospecific vs polyspecific DAT?

 

●      Coombs reagents are of two types:

○      1. Monospecific Coombs reagent:

■      Contains only one specificity: either anti-IgG or anti-C3d in the gel matrix

○      2. Polyspecific Coombs reagent:

■      Contains both anti-IgG and anti-C3d (complement) in the gel matrix

■      May be used as an initial screen

Q. Technical reasons for a false negative DAT?

●      Will depend on tube testing vs gel card (gel cards already contain AHG)

●      Think: preanalytical, analytical, post analytical phases

●      Wrong patient

●      Timing too long (ab dissociates)

●      Over/under centrifuge

●      Missed AHG (if tube testing)

●      Expired AHG

●      Too weak suspension

●      Over centrifuge, under centrifuge

●      Interpretation or transcription error

Q. What are 4 causes of a false negative DAT? (SMH)

●      Prozone effect (antibody titre is too high)

●      Low titre antibody below assay sensitivity to detect

●      Low avidity/affinity antibody

●      IgA antibody

●      Severe hemolysis and clearance of cells

Q. What is the prozone/postzone effect?

·       The “hook effect” or the “prozone effect” → a type of interference which plagues certain immunoassays and nephelometric assays

·       It occurs due to a high antibody titer → which interferes with formation of antigen- antibody lattice, which is necessary to visualize a positive test

·       This results in → false negatives or inaccurately low results

 

Q. 5 causes of a (true) positive DAT?

●      Non-specific autoantibody

●      Alloantibodies reacting with recently-transfused donor red cells

●      Alloantibodies from donor plasma reacting with recipient red cells 

○      Transfusion of high-titre group O platelets to A / B / AB individuals

○      IVIG administration

●      Maternal alloantibodies coating fetal red cells

●      Passenger lymphocyte syndrome (donor lymphocytes producing antibodies against recipient red cells)

●      Drug-induced haemolytic anaemia

●      Monoclonal antibodies bound to RBC surface (e.g. daratumumab)

●      Paraproteins with hypergammaglobulinaemia

●      Antithymocyte globulin

●      Can be seen in healthy individuals (1:7000)

●      Next steps:

○      Obtain drug history

○      Obtain transfusion history

○      Eluate

 

From ExpertPath

·       Clinically significant causes

o   Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia

o   Drug-induced hemolytic anemia (all forms)

o   Acute or delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions

o   Cold agglutinin disease

o   Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria

o   Hemolytic disease of fetus and newborn

o   Passenger lymphocyte syndrome

o   Passively transfused clinically significant antibodies (causes hemolysis) in plasma (from plasma/platelets, Rh immune globulin, or IVIG)

 

 

Q. Expected DAT & eluate results in cold agglutinin syndrome?

●      Positive for C3d, negative for IgG.

●      Eluate is non-reactive

Q. Describe the DAT & eluate findings in drug induced hemolytic anemia?

●      DAT positive for IgG alone

●      Eluate is non-reactive

Q. What are 2 general types of atypical AIHA?

●      AIHA with a Negative DAT

●      Warm Antibody AIHA Caused by IgM or IgA Autoantibodies

Q. How do you diagnose a DAT negative AIHA?

·       This is a clinical diagnosis

·       Need evidence indicative of acquired hemolytic anemia.

·       DAT negative with anti-IgG/anti-C3d

·       No unexpected antibodies detectable in serum or eluate (sometimes antibody can be detected in eluate)

·       Responds to prednisone treatment

Q. Compare intravascular vs extravascular hemolysis - give the expected laboratory results for each?

·       Intravascular → schistocytes, decrease haptoglobin, urine hemoglobin and hemosiderin positive, DAT negative and LDH increased

·       Extravascular → spherocytes, mild decrease haptoglobin, urine hemoglobin and hemosiderin negative, DAT positive, LDH increased
