Q. How does an autocontrol differ from a DAT?

●      Autocontrol has patient plasma and cells

●      DAT is just the patients red cells and AHG

●      Temperature at which they are run at is the main difference

○      AC: 37C incubation

○      DAT: Room temp 18 - 24 with and AHG

Q. What are causes of differences in positivity between DAT and auto control - eg Positive autocontrol/negative DAT and Negative autocontrol/positive DAT combinations?

 

Autocontrol does not always EQUAL the DAT:

●      Positive autocontrol/negative DAT

○      1) Agglutination in the autocontrol is dependent on the enhancement media picking up nonspecific binding or very weak specific binding

○      2) Improper techniques leading to a false negative DAT

○      3) Preservative dependent reactivity

●      Negative autocontrol/positive DAT:

○      1) Temperature: Autocontrol is performed at 37C → this may result in the elution of the antibody from the red cells particularly if it is a low avidity antibody

Q. What 2 antigens require a negative DAT in order to test for them?

 

●      Duffy and S s

○      These anti-sera reagents use an IgG thus you require an AHG phase to agglutinate (ie. an IAT phase)

○      If the patient has a positive DAT, they will look positive for these antigens!

○      Positive DAT means sensitized RBCs which will be agglutinated by the AHG at 37 regardless of the anti-sera being bound

Q. Why must the DAT be negative for Duffy and S s testing? ?cellano

●      They are the only ones done by IAT.

●      Others are immediate spin tests at room temperature

●      To resolve → you can treat with EGA (EGA = EDTA plus acid glycine) and do IAT, but this can be unreliable

●      EGA removes bound ab from patient cells

Q. What are 3 causes of positive cord blood DAT?

 

●      Cord blood = fetal RBCs

●      ABO incompatibility

○      #1 reason

○      If mom is group O (anti-A, anti-B IgG) & baby is group A, B or AB

●      Maternal alloimmunization/alloantibodies

○      ? HDFN (eg anti-D in a D neg mother with D pos baby)

○      ? RhIg

●      Maternal autoantibodies

●      Drugs

●      Wharton’s Jelly?

 

Q. What is IAT?

·       What antibodies are in my patients plasma?

 

5.Antibody Panels and identification

 

Q. What are 4 common egs in blood banking where an IAT is used?

  1. Forward and reverse blood group testing
  2. Antibody screen
  3. Antibody identification panel
  4. The crossmatch

●      Uses

○      Patient → plasma/serum containing abs

○      Reagent/donor → red cells as the antigen source

 

Q. What are check cells and when are they used in IAT?

●      Check cells are IgG coated/sensitized RBCs

●      You add 1 drop of IgG-coated control cells check cells to each negative tube to make sure you didn’t forget to add the AHG reagent (check cells should produce a positive agglutination result)

 

Q. Describe how to do SIAT testing (saline indirect antiglobulin testing by tube method)?

·       IAT → method used in both forward and reverse blood group testing, the antibody screen, the antibody identification panel and the crossmatch using

o   Patient → plasma/serum

o   Reagent/donor → red cells

●      A separate plasma and an aliquot of red cells are placed into the appropriately labelled tubes.

●      Prepare a 3-5% saline suspension of patient’s red cells to be used for the auto control → if an antibody identification panel is being performed.

●      1. Add 1 drop of 3-5% suspension of reagent red cells to the corresponding tube

○      Wash the red cells once with saline in an automatic cell washer or by hand to form a dry cell button.

●      2. Add 6 drops of patient's cell-free plasma to each tube.

○      Mix well, ensuring that the cell button is completely re-suspended.

○      Incubate tubes for 30 minutes in a 37+2ºC water bath.

●      3. Remove tubes from the water bath and centrifuge for 1 minute and 10 seconds at 2250 rpm (low speed).

○      Read tube macroscopically for agglutination

●      4. Wash red cells four times with saline in an automatic cell washer or by hand to form a dry cell button.

●      5. Add 2 drops of anti-IgG to each tube. Mix contents, spin for 1 minute and 10 seconds at 2250 rpm (low speed).

○      Read macroscopically and record results.

●      6. Add 1 drop of IgG-coated control cells (check cells, which are sensitized RBCs) to each negative tube. Spin for 30 seconds at 3400 rpm (high speed). Read and record results.

○      At least a 2+ positives reaction must be obtained to ensure the validity of the test results

 

Q. What is a cause of false positive in SIAT testing related to the testing method?

●      False-positive results may occur → if antibodies to components of the preservative solution are present in the plasma tested.

●      Significant variations in red blood cell suspensions may result in false-positive or false-negative reactions.

Q. What is a positive test result in SIAT?

●      Two things may indicate a positive result → hemolysis or agglutination

●      Hemolysis or agglutination indicates the presence of an antibody directed against the corresponding antigen, which is present on the screening cells and/or antibody panel cells.

Q. How is positivity graded in SIAT (test tubes)?

 

 

●      Either a 0 - 4 or 0 - 12 scale

●      0 = No agglutinates, even RBC suspension

●      1 = Small agglutinates with a lot of free RBCs in background

●      2 = Medium sized agglutinates, clear background

●      3 = One to two large agglutinates, clear background, strong reaction

●      4 = One solid agglutinate, clear background/no free RBCs detected

Q. How does gel testing work?

●      You incubate your red cells (0.8% suspension) and plasma 1st, and then add them to the reaction chamber (?)

●      Then you centrifuge → which forces cells through the gel

●      The gel contains your anti-IgG or IgM antibodies impregnated in them.

Q. How do gel cards separate positive and negative reactions?

●      1) Microtubules/columns are filled with gel & anti-IgG or anti-IgM reagent abs

●      2) Gel particles → separate red cell clusters by size

●      3) Anti-IgG/M → grabs onto red cells coated by Ig (sensitized RBCs)

●      4) Bigger red cell agglutination will be stuck higher in gel

●      5) Negative gel tests → show cells in a button at the bottom

●      6) Positive gel tests → show cells spread in varying degrees through the microtube

Q. How is screening done by gel cards?

·       1) Add reagent screening RBCs → 50 uL of each 3-cell 0.8% antibody screening cell suspension to the upper well of the appropriate microtube of the MTS anti-IgG cards

·       2) Add patient/recipient plasma → 25uL of recipient plasma to the appropriate microtube of MTS anti-IgG cards

·       3) Incubate → the MTS anti-IgG cards at 37 +/-2C for 15 minutes in the MTS incubator (must incubate first to sensitize RBCs before centrifuging)

·       4) Centrifuge → Transfer the MTS anti-IgG cards to MTS centrifuge ensuring they are properly balanced and run for 10 minutes at 900rpm

·       Read → the front and back of each MTS anti-IgG cards microtube macroscopically for agglutination and/or hemolysis.

 

Q. What type of cards do crossmatch, antibody screening, and antibody identification testing all use?

·       All use cards containing → dextran acrylamide gel with anti-IgG impregnated in it.

Q. What is the correct order of adding reagents to the gel cards - why is this important?

·       1) Must add red cells first.

·       2) Add serum or plasma second (containing ab)

·       If you add plasma 1st → it moves down through gel card before red cells are added and can be sensitized. The plasma wouldn't stay in reaction chamber = possible false negative reaction

Q. What are false positive causes of reactivity with a gel card?

●      Anomalous results may be caused by:

○      Fresh serum/plasma

○      Fibrin in the serum or plasma (clotted specimen)

○      Particulate matter in the serum or plasma

○      RBCs that stick to the sides of the micro-tube.

○      Rouleaux (paraprotein in plasma)

○      Lipemic samples can cause false positives.

○      Think of other stuff that can be in the plasma causing RBC clumping

●      Anomalous results with fresh serum (i.e. a line of red cells on top of the gel) may be minimized by the use of EDTA plasma

Q. How is positivity graded in the Gel cards - what are the possible results?

●      MF - RBC agglutination noted on the top of the gel accompanied by a button of un-agglutinated RBC in the bottom of the microtube (combination of 0 & 4+)

●      0 - well-defined RBC button in the bottom of the microtube with no agglutinins seen in the gel microtube

●      1+ - RBC agglutinates observed in the lower half of the gel microtube

●      2+ - RBC agglutinates dispersed throughout the length of the gel microtube

●      3+ - RBC agglutinates observed in the upper half of the gel microtube

●      4+ - RBC agglutinates form a solid band at the top of the gel microtube

Q. Compare and contrast gel vs tube technique - give advantages and disadvantages for gel?

 

1) Advantages:

●      Easier to standardize (reproducible, reduced subjectivity, reduced operator variability)

●      No wash steps

●      Stable reaction for 48-72 hours - may be reviewed later

●      Decreased sample volumes needed.

●      No need for antiglobulin control cells (check cells)

●      Can be automated - requires less tech time

●      Higher sensitivity and specificity.

2) Disadvantages:

●      Higher cost per test/more expensive

●      Special equipment needed (incubator, centrifuge, workstations/racks)

 

Q. Causes for false negatives in IATs and DATs

·       Cells not washed adequately

·       Inadequate resuspension of RBCs between washes

·       Leaving cells in saline for too long

·       Deterioration of AHG in storage

·       Failure to add AHG to test

·       Delay in adding AHG to washed cells

·       Under or over centrifugation

·       Too many or too few RBCs

·       Too high or too low IgG concentration in patient plasma

·       Improper storage of RBCs/serum

·       Antibody that doesn't react to specific AHG

·       Improper incubation

·       Patient serum not added

·       Poor reading

Elution

Q. What is an elution?

●      Elution = a technique where you strip antibodies from a patient’s cells and then test those antibodies against panel cells to see if the ab has specificity.

●      The removal of antibody coating the surface of a patient’s red blood cells through physical or chemical means

Q. What do you call the solution that is available for analysis after an elution is performed?

 

●      Called the “eluate” in blood bank language

Q. When do you perform elution?

●      When the DAT is positive by IgG

○      HDFN

○      Transfusion reaction

○      Autoimmune disease

●      C3d is IgM mediated primarily → these antibodies are not detectable in the eluate

 

●      UHN Protocol: Test the Eluate of patients who have a positive DAT due to anti-IgG and one of the following criteria:

○      Recently transfused within the last 3 months

○      Clinical evidence of hemolysis

○      AIHA (not routinely done, may be requested by a physician or senior staff).

○      Drug induced hemolytic anemia (requested by a physician or senior staff)

○      DAT is newly positive, when the patient is either anemic (Hb < 100g/L) or is requiring a red cell transfusion.

○      For a patient with a positive DAT due to complement only where there is a suspected presence of a complement binding antibody e.g. the Kidd system

Q. What elution Methods are available?

·       Acid elutions (glycine acid) 

o   Most common 

o   Lowers pH, causing antibody to dissociate 

·       Organic solvents (ether, chloroform) 

o   Dissolve bilipid layer of RBC 

·       Heat (conformational change) 

·       Freeze-Thaw (lyses cells)

 

Q. What is the most common solution used to perform an elution?

●      Acidic glycine solution (ie. EGA - EDTA Glycine Acid)

Q. What can’t you do in elution?

·       Do not add LISS, PEG or any other potentiators to either the Eluate or the last wash tubes

·       Do not test eluates using Gel

·       Do not use pre-warm technique for testing eluates

 

Q. Defining the cause of a DAT with elution

•        Positive eluate

–       Autoantibody – usually panagglutinin

–       Alloantibody – RBC Ag specific

•        Negative Eluate

–       Drug

–      
 anti-A or anti-B (unless test with A or B cells)

Eluate during acute alloantibody formation


Eluate in drug-induced hemolysis

Eluate: Warm autoantibody

Pattern: panaggulitin

 

Q. Why it is important to identify autoantibodies?

·       Autoantibodies can sometimes “mask” clinically significant alloantibodies, so it’s important to differentiate between  auto- and allo-antibodies

Q. What are the features of cold autoantibodies?

·       React at room temperature with most (if not all) of the panel cells and give a positive autocontrol 

·       The DAT is usually positive with anti-C3 AHG (detects complement) 

·       Could be due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae, infectious mono, or cold agglutinin disease

·       Mini-cold panels can be used to help identify cold autoantibodies

·       Since anti-I is a common autoantibody, cord blood cells (no I antigen) are usually included

 

Q. What other techniques can be used if the cold antibodies remain?

·       Prewarmed techniques can be performed: 

o   Red cells, serum, and saline are incubated at 37° before being combined

·       Autoadsorption is another technique in which the autoantibody is removed from the patients serum using their own red cells 

o   The serum can be used to identify any underlying alloantibodies

Adsorption

What are the three types of adsorptions?

·       Autoadsorption → patients own RBCs (cannot have been transfused in the last 3 months) -> Autoantibodies are removed using patient RBCs, so alloantibodies can be identified

·       Alloadsorption → reagent cells with known phenotype, choosing combination of cells with different antigen expression. Use if recent transfusion (last 3 months) -> Uses other cells with the patients serum

·       Homologous adsorption

Q. What is a homologous adsorption - for what type of patient is this theoretically useful for?

●      Used in patients who have been previously phenotyped

●      The adsorption is performed using phenotypically matched red cells instead of the patient’s own cells (autoadsorption). The RBCs you use have the same phenotype as the patient

●      In theory this technique can be used in severely anemic patients when you want to minimize blood draws

Q. When is an alloadsorption used?

●      Alloadsorption may be used when a patient has been transfused in the last 3 months (which is a contraindication for an autoadsorption)

●      Alloadsorption uses red cells with a known phenotype to remove reactivity from a sample to allow clarification of antibody specificity in patients who have complex antibody panels likely caused by multiple antibodies.

Q. What reagent is used to remove bound antibody from the red cell surface prior to doing an adsorption?

·       EGA → EDTA plus acidic glycine solution

o   Favoured option

·       ZZAP solution → which is a mixture of dithiothreitol (DTT) and papain

o   Downside: DTT degrades Kell

o   Cannot exclude presence of an anti Kell antibody, so must provide Kell negative blood

o   Makes this less favourable

Q. How do you do autoadsorption?

Q. What is the “last wash” in blood banking?

·       When you do an elution, you wash away the plasma that the red cells are suspended in 3 or 4 times → the last wash is the run on the panel cells → you expect it to be negative (all unbound circulating antibodies in patient plasma were removed) → otherwise the test is void

·       Washing is done → to remove any free circulating antibodies in the patients plasma, before adding acidic glycine to strip bound antibodies off the red cells and test those antibodies (the eluate) on the panel

·       You want to know the specificity of the bound abs, causing the positive DAT, not the specificity of any unbound circulating antibodies

·       You test the last wash to ensure that it's negative against the antibody screen panel so you're sure the antibodies from the patient’s plasma aren't contaminating your eluate antibodies (antibodies that were coating the patient’s RBCs)

Q. What are 3 methods to remove interference from cold agglutinins (IgM) in blood banking?

 

●      Pre-warm

●      Treat serum/plasma with DTT (denatures IgM by destroying disulphide bonds; also destroys Kell)

●      REST (rabbit erythrocyte stroma)

●      Cold adsorption techniques:

○      Autologous adsorption → if patient has not been recently transfused

○      Alloadsorption → as in WAIHA (rarely necessary)

Q. What is REST used for in blood banking?

●      Rabbit erythrocyte stroma are known to → adsorb IgM antibodies from plasma

●      There is some concern they may remove/reduce titres of clinically significant IgM and IgG antibodies as well.

Q. What are the requirements to do a RBC phenotype?

●      Cannot be transfused in past 90 days / 3 months

●      DAT is negative by gel (either card or provue method)

●      If positive in gel can strip antibodies from cell and do phenotype by tube method

Q. What is the concordance of genotyping with antigenic typing in blood transfusion?

●      0.9997

●      Casas J, Friedman DF, Jackson T, et al. Changing practice: red blood cell typing by molecular methods for patients with sickle cell disease. Transfusion 2015;55:000-00.

Q. What are lectins, give 3 examples of their use in blood bank:

·       Dolichos biflorus → anti-A1 specificity (agglutinates A1 RBCs, but not A2)

·       Ulex europaeus → anti-H specificity

·       Vicia graminea → anti-N specificity

·       Glycine max → Polyagglutination - specificity

Q. What enzymes can treat red cells - name 4?

●      Most commonly use ficin, but can use papain, bromelin, or trypsin.

Q. Enzyme enhanced antigens?

●      ABO/H systems

●      Kidd System

●      Lewis system

●      I system

●      Rh System

●      P system

●      “Lewis P Is A Rhotten Kidd”

Q. Antigens inactivated by enzyme treatment?

●      Duffy, MNS (some degree of s) and Lutheran

●      Mainly Duffy and MNS, but also can be Xga, Chido, Rogers

●      Enzyme destroys Duffy and minimize MNS.

Q. Antigens unaffected by enzyme treatment?

●      Kell

●      Diego

●      Colton

Q. Antigens destroyed by sulfhydryl reagents

·       Kell

Q. Antigens that exhibit dosage

·       Rh

·       Kidd

·       Lutheran

·       Duffy

·       MN

·       Ss

Q. What is the monocyte monolayer assay?

●      Essentially a way to create a false reticuloendothelial system to determine if an antibody is going to be clinically significant

●      An assay where the patient’s antibodies (plasma) and patient monocytes are put on a slide with the donor red cells.

●      Under a microscope the number of red cells adhering to or engulfed by monocytes is graded → to predict whether the patient will hemolyze the red cells if transfused.

Q. What are the causes of a pan-reactive antibody?

Allo

1.     A single alloAb to a high incidence Ag, ie. anti-JK3

2.     2 or more alloAb react at same strength, ie. Anti-e, anti-Fyb, anti-Jka

3.     Multiple alloAb including high titer low affinity HTLA Ab

4.     A combination of above

5.     Warm or cold reactive alloAb

6.     Passive transferred Ab, ie. IVIG

Auto

7.     Warm reactive autoantibody

8.     AIHA

 

Q. What steps can you take to work up a pan-reactive antibody investigation with a negative auto-control?

●      DDx: multiple alloantibodies or single alloantibody against a high frequency antigen

●      Test plasma against cells negative for high incidence antigens

●      Set up enzyme panel

●      SIAT or prewarmed SIAT (saline‐indirect antiglobulin test)

●      Test using made up cells (re-suspended in fresh diluent to desired concentration)

Note: solid phase testing review is not included

 

How do I determine how many units to screen when a clinically significant antibody is detected?

·       Need to know incidence of antigens

·       Example: Pt has anti K and needs 4 units RBC

·       K - incidence is 90% = 0.90

·       4 units K- blood needed   = 4.4 units

·       0.90

6.Massive Hemorrhage Protocol MHP

 

Q. What is massive transfusion definition?

●      Retrospective definitions

○      Administration of 10 units or transfusing more than one blood volume in 24h period (Bloody Easy 5th).

●      Dynamic definitions

○      Transfusion of 3 units of pRBC within 1h with ongoing need anticipated (by Massive hemorrhage and emergency transfusion | Professional Education (blood.ca))

○      UHN MHP: 4 units within 1 hour

○      Pediatric definition:

■      Transfusion support to replace ongoing blood loss of >10% total blood volume (TBV) per min

■      Transfusion >100% TBV in 24 hours

■      Transfusion >50% TBV in 3 hours

Q. What are underlying physiologic factors that contribute to Massive Transfusion bleeding?

1. Loss of clotting factors from bleeding

2. Activation of coagulation by traumatic exposure of subendothelium

3. Dilutional coagulopathy

4. Some fluids (hypertonic saline) appear to have anticoagulatory and anti-platelet effects

5. Exposure of tissue t-PA plasminogen activator causing hyperfibrinolysis

6. Hypothermia

7. Acidosis (decreases fibrin polymerization)

8. Acute traumatic coagulopathy

 

Q. What is acute traumatic coagulopathy?

●      An impairment in hemostasis that is independent of factors listed above that is observed in major injury.

●      Etiology is unclear but may be protein C mediated: endogenous anticoagulation, enhanced fibrinolysis

 

Q. What is the effect of hypothermia on coagulation?

●      1) Reduces enzymatic function of some coagulation proteins (serine proteases)

●      2) Impairs interaction of vWF with platelets

●      Bleeding is the common result

Q. What is the relationship between acidosis and coagulation?

●      1) Impairs the formation of the tenase and prothrombinase complexes on platelet surfaces

●      2) Decreases fibrin polymerization

●      Bleeding is the common result

Q. What is our initial transfusion management of massive transfusion?

●      The initial management of the rapidly bleeding patient that precludes the use of laboratory-guided transfusion should begin with immediate red blood cell (RBC) transfusion and then transfusions at a RBC:plasma ratio of 2:1.

[QZ1] [QZ2] [QZ3] 

Q. what is the minimal laboratory protocol resuscitation targets for MHP transfusion?

●      (1) hemoglobin >80 g/L (RBC);

●      (2) INR <1.8 (plasma or prothrombin complex concentrates);

●      (3) Fibrinogen >1.5 g/L (cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrates[QZ4] );

●      (4) platelets [QZ5] > 50 x109/L; UHN: >100 if CNS injury or patient on ECLS circuit

●      (5) ionized calcium [QZ6] >1.15 mmol/L.

●      Relevant transfusion targets can also be used if viscoelastic testing is performed.

Q. What is a reasonable alternative to cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen replacement?

●      Fibrinogen concentrate 4 grams (equivalent to approx. 10 u of cryo)

Q. At institutions lacking sufficient resources to issue plasma (e.g., no thawing device or no plasma stocked in inventory), Prothrombin Complex Concentrates (PCC) 2000 IU can be substituted for coagulation factor replacement. what should be given concurrently with PCCs unless the fibrinogen level is known to be >1.5g/L?

●      Fibrinogen replacement with fibrinogen concentrate FC

Q. Tranexamic acid should be administered as soon as intravenous or intraosseous access is achieved but within ?-hours from time of injury or within ?-hours from MHP activation in all other patients.

●      3-hours; 3-hours

●      UHN MHP: IV TXA 10 mg per kg bolus over 15 min, followed by 1 mg per kg per h infusion to max 10 hours, if within 3 hours of onset of hemorrhage; simplified protocol for average-sized adult: 1 g over 10 min and then another 1 g over 8 hours

Q. What is the name of the trial comparing 1:1:1 vs 1:1:2?

●      PROPPR trial in JAMA

●      doi:10.1001/jama.2015.12

●      Intervention

○      Blood product ratios of 1:1:1 (plasma:plts:RBCs)

○      Packs contained 6 U plasma, 1 dose plts (pool of 6 U) and 6 U RBCs

●      Control

○      Blood product ratios of 1:1:2 (plasma:plts:RBCs)

○      Alternating packs containing 3 U plasma, 0 dose plts and 6 U RBCs with 3 U plasma, 1 dose plts and 6 U RBCs

 

Q. What were the findings of the PROPRR trial?

●      Found that at 3 hours 1:1:1 led to reduced hemorrhagic mortality when compared to 1:1:2.

●      No difference in overall mortality at 24 hours or 30 days.

Q. What is a 1:1:1 ratio of blood products in Canada?

●      1U Platelets/4U plasma/4U RBC? - CHECK THIS!

Q. Can you issue A, B, or AB blood product in massive transfusion based on a historical/previous ABO Rh typing?

·       No → you must only give this product if typing is available at that time, otherwise O- or O+ product has to be issued

·       Switch to group specific product as soon as typing results are available

Q. What storage solution do we use for RBC?

·       Citrate phosphate dextrose (CPD) → 21 days

·       Citrate phosphate dextrose adenine (CPDA) → 35 days

·       CPDA and additive (saline, adenine, dextrose & mannitol [SAGM]) → 42 days

Q. What are the complications of citrate infusion in massive transfusion (2)?

●      Large amounts of citrate are given with massive blood transfusion, since blood is anticoagulated with sodium citrate and citric acid.

●      Two potential complications of citrate infusion and accumulation:

○      Metabolic alkalosis → from citrate metabolism in liver

○      Hypocalcemia → citrate chelates plasma calcium = a decline in the plasma free calcium concentration

Q. What is the cause and concern with hypocalcemia in massive transfusion?

●      Citrate binding of ionized calcium can lead to a clinically significant fall in the plasma free calcium concentration.

●      This change can lead to → paresthesias and/or cardiac arrhythmias in some patients

Q. What is the role of lab testing in massive transfusion?

●      The recommended minimum laboratory testing (where the test is available) at each blood draw should be: CBC, INR, activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT; baseline only), fibrinogen, electrolytes, calcium (ionized), blood gas (pH and base excess) and lactate.

●      No evidence for ROTEM, TEG, or traditional labs techniques (PTT, INR, CBC, or fibrinogen)

●      Recommended lab tests be done q1h

●      UHN MHP states:

○      CBC, aPTT (baseline only), INR, fibrinogen, arterial blood gas q60 minutes (minimum)

○      electrolytes, serum creatinine, ALT, ionized Ca, Mg, serum lactate q4hours or following every 20 blood components administered (minimum)

 

 

 

Jeanie Callum notes on MHP

  1. Evidence-Based Practice:
    • Emphasizes restrictive transfusion strategies (Hb <70–80 g/L) over liberal approaches (Hb <90–100 g/L) based on 34 RCTs (22,943 patients).
    • No mortality benefit for liberal strategies in most cases, including cardiac surgery (TRICS III) and acute MI (REALITY Trial).
  1. Critical Trials & Outcomes:
    • TRICC Study (ICU patients): Restrictive (Hb <70 g/L) reduced in-hospital mortality (22.2% vs. 28.1%, P=0.05).
    • Villanueva Trial (UGIB): Restrictive strategy (Hb <70 g/L) improved survival (95% vs. 91%, P=0.02) and reduced rebleeding.
    • AABB Guidelines (2016):
      • <70 g/L for stable inpatients.
      • <80 g/L for cardiac/orthopedic surgery.
  1. Risks of Transfusion:
    • TACO (1 in 50–100) and TRALI (1 in 10,000) are top risks.
    • Infection transmission (e.g., HIV: 1 in 21 million) is rare.
    • Liberal strategies correlate with higher mortality and adverse events.
  1. Pre-Transfusion Checklist:
    • Alternatives first: Iron, B12, or erythropoietin.
    • Consent: Disclose risks (TACO, hemolysis, TRALI).
    • Special populations:
      • Females <45: Kell-negative units to prevent HDFN.
      • Immunocompromised: Irradiated blood.
      • High TACO risk: Diuretics for age ≥70, CHF, or renal dysfunction.
  1. Patient-Specific Triggers:

Scenario

Threshold

Action

Asymptomatic young patient

<50 g/L

1 unit

Cardiac history

<70–80 g/L

1 unit

Acute MI (asymptomatic)

<80 g/L

1 unit, slow infusion

Rapid hemorrhage

Keep 60–110 g/L

Uncrossmatched units as needed
  1. Donor Considerations:
    • 65.9% of female donors (Hb 125–129 g/L) have iron deficiency (ferritin <25 µg/L).
    • Minimize transfusions to protect donor health.
  1. 2021 Recommendations:
    • Prioritize iron therapy over transfusion for iron-deficient patients.
    • Avoid transfusions in young women to reduce alloimmunization risk.
    • Transfuse 1 unit at a time (unless active bleeding) and reassess post-transfusion.

 

7.How to administer blood products

Q. Samples submitted for pretransfusion testing must include what information?

●      2 independent identifiers (Name, DOB, unique hospital number)

●      Date of draw

●      Means of identifying person who drew the sample (signature or initials)

●      Patient data must be taken from patient arm/wrist band and label must completed and affixed to sample at the bedside.

Q. Historical records must be reviewed for what 5 things in blood banking?

●      1) ABO and Rh typing

●      2) Difficulty in blood typing

●      3) Clinically significant antibodies

●      4) Significant adverse events to transfusion

●      5) Special transfusion requirements.

Q. How long is a test sample good for prior to transfusion

●      Outpatient:

○      3 days if pregnant or transfused in the past 3 months or has a history of antibodies

○      Otherwise some institutions respect results up to 30-45 days old eg if drawn as an outpatient in a pre-assessment clinic prior to an elective surgery

●      Inpatient:

○      96 hours for inpatients!!

Q. What must be done when blood products are issued from the blood bank - the “final check”?

●      At the time a unit is issued there shall be a final check of transfusion service records and each unit of blood or blood component.

●      Verification shall include:

○      1) The intended recipients 2 independant identifiers, ABO group, and Rh type

○      2) The donation identification number, the donor ABO group and Rh type

○      3) The interpretation of crossmatch results if performed.

○      4) Special transfusion requirements if applicable.

○      5) Expiration date and time

○      6) Date and time of issue.

Q. What must blood products be visually inspected for prior to release for transfusion or shipment?

●      Contamination

●      Leakage

●      Inadequate seals

●      Abnormal appearance

●      RBC containing components must be examined for hemolysis, visible clots, abnormal coloring (red, brown, purple) of the plasma or supernatant or turbidity.

●      Any of these changes suggest contamination.

●      Highly lipemic (milky colored) units are not suitable for transfusion

What is the maximum allowable transport temperature for an RBC unit?

●      10 C

Q. When must RBC units must be transfused after leaving the blood bank, and how long can they be gone and accepted back?

●      Must be transfused within 4 hours of issue from transfusion service.

●      Can only be returned to transfusion service if within 30 minutes.

●      Rationale is that if more than 30 minutes, the unit may have exceeded maximum allowable transport temperature (10 C) which puts the unit at risk of bacterial contamination

Q. What are the requirements of a computer crossmatch?

●      1. Computer system has been validated on site to ensure that only ABO compatible RBC components are selected for transfusion.

●      2. Two determinations of the recipients ABO group have been made. One on a current sample and a second by one of the following methods: by retesting the same sample, by testing a second current sample, or by comparison with previous records.

●      3. The system contains the donation ID number, component name, ABO and Rh type, confirmed ABO group, two unique recipient numbers, recipient ABO and Rh type, antibody screen results and interpretation of compatibility.

●      4. A method exists to verify correct entry of data before release of blood components.

●      5. The system contains logic to alert the user to discrepancies between the donor and recipient.     

Another answer:

●      1. Two determinations of the recipients ABO group have been made. One on a current sample and a second by one of the following methods: by retesting the same sample, by testing a second current sample, or by comparison with previous records.

●      2. Negative antibody screen and no Hx of clinically significant antibody in the recipient

●      3. Two separate ABO determinations on donor unit, one at CBS, the other at receiving hospital

●      4. Computer system has been validated on site to ensure that only ABO compatible RBC components are selected for transfusion.

●      5. The system contains logic to alert the user to discrepancies between the donor and recipient.

Q. How many people must verify the unit and patient before transfusion?

●      2 people, one of whom is the transfusionist

Q. What is the typical reaction reported with the use of bedside leukoreduction?

●      Severe hypotension that typically resolves with discontinuation of transfusion.

●      Rare though with only around 100 cases reported.

Q. What are 2 main concerns in the pre-transplant period with regards to transfusion approach?

●      Minimize HLA alloimmunization

●      Prevent TA-GVHD (recipient is immunocompromised)

 

Q. What are the four main issues with ABO mismatch in SCT?

 

●      Antibodies

○      Stay around for many weeks’ post-transplant

○      Destroy red cells and precursors

●      Four main issues:

○      1. Delayed red cell engraftment

○      2. Increased RBC transfusion requirements

○      3. Pure red cell aplasia

○      4. Post- transplant hemolysis

Q. What is the general approach to transfusion for red cells and plasma after SCT?

●      Majority of patients are transfused O red cells and AB plasma

●      Note: this may not be the most correct answer!

●      This is the easy and lazy way to provide blood products!

●      See below

Q. What is a minor mismatch?

●      donor B lymphocytes to produce anti-recipient antibodies (e.g. group O donor to a group A recipient)

Q. What is a major mismatch?

●      anti-donor ABO antibodies are present in the recipient (e.g. group A donor to a group O recipient)

Q. What is a Bi-directional ABO mismatch?

●      both donor and recipient have antibodies directed against ABO blood group antigens of each other (e.g. group A donor to a group B recipient)

https://doi.org/10.1159/000441507

Q. What is approach to transfusion product selection in minor ABO incompatible SCT?

●      Transfuse the donor’s RBC type (or group O) and recipient’s FFP/platelet type (or AB)

●      In minor mismatch, the ab is in the donor product

Q. What is approach to transfusion with major ABO incompatibility in SCT?

●      Transfuse the recipient’s RBC type (or group O) and donor’s FFP/platelet type (or group AB)

●      In major mismatch, the ab is in the recipient plasma

Q. What are four possible indications for albumin?

●      Paracentesis (large volume)

●      Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

●      Hepatorenal syndrome

●      Plasma exchange replacement fluid

Q. What are common platelet transfusion thresholds?

●      Keep

●      >10 for normal patients

●      >20 fever or coagulopathy

●      >20-50 procedures not associated with blood loss (eg central line placement)

●      >80 epidural or lumbar anesthesia

●      >50 procedure with blood loss or major surgery

●      >100 neurosurgery or head trauma

 

Q. What are general transfusion guidelines for PLTs in infants?

●      There is very poor evidence and practice varies dramatically. Generally though:

○      Stable infant <20k

○      Unstable infant <30-50k

○      Bleeding infant or procedure <50k

Q. What are 5 contraindications to Platelet transfusion?

●      HIT

●      TTP

●      ITP

●      Post transfusion purpura (PTP)

●      Uremic bleeding??

Q. What are 3 indications for washed platelets?

●      1) NAIT with maternal PLT transfusion:

○      This procedure may be indicated in the clinical setting of neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia where maternal platelets are collected and washed to remove anti-HPA-1a (HPA-1a causes 75-80% of FNAIT in White patients).

●      2) IgA deficiency:

○      Washed platelets are also used for IgA deficient patients with documented anti-IgA when platelets from an IgA deficient donor are unavailable

●      3) Anaphylaxis:

○      Patients with a history of anaphylaxis of unknown etiology associated with previous blood transfusions.

What are two ways to provide PLTs to a patient with IgA deficiency & documented anti-IgA antibody?

●      Single donor apheresis collection from an IgA deficient donor

●      Washed PLTs

Q. What are 3 indications for washed red cells?

●      Prevention of anaphylaxis caused by antibodies against plasma proteins (IgA deficient)

●      Intrauterine transfusion

●      Prevention of febrile transfusion reactions

●      Prevention of urticarial transfusion reactions

Q. Intravenous fluid use with RBC transfusion - what are 2 acceptable fluids?

●      Should technically only use 0.9% NS or 5% albumin to simplify process and ensure no errors.

●      Caution when use products which contain calcium like ringers that could in theory reverse anticoagulation and cause clotting

●      Dextrose and hypotonic saline → will cause hemolysis.

●      Few other solutions are FDA approved (normosol-R, plasma-lyte A injection).

Q. What is the standard volume of RBC transfusion for infants and small children?

●      10-15 ml/kg increases Hgb 20-30g/l depending on hematocrit and storage solution.

Q. When are vitals taken during transfusion?

●      Time 0

●      Time 15 minutes

●      End

●      At the time of any subsequent transfusion reaction

Q. When should patients be monitored during transfusion?

●      Before starting the transfusion (baseline observation)

●      15 minutes after starting the transfusion

●      At least every hour during transfusion

●      Carry out a final set of observations 15 minutes after each unit has been transfused

 

Q. When should post transfusion hemoglobin be measured?

●      The post-transfusion hemoglobin level may be accurately measured as early as 15 minutes following transfusion.

8.Leukocyte reduction, irradiation, and bacterial testing

 

Q. Why is universal leukocyte reduction mandated in the UK and Canada?

●      vCJD prion protein prevention

●      vCJD prion protein is noted to be high in lymphoid tissues in infected patients.

●      Felt that leukoreduction could reduce risk.

●      The US minimizes risk with strict donor deferral rather than leukocyte reduction

Q. What are five methods of leukocyte reduction?

●      Prestorage filtration

●      Bedside filtration

●      Saline Washing

●      Freezing and deglycerolization

●      Centrifugation

Q. What are benefits of leukocyte reduction?

●      Risk of CMV, HTLV, and EBV decreased

●      Decreased HLA alloimmunization

●      Decreased PLT refractoriness

●      Decrease FNHTR

●      Decrease transfusion related immunomodulation (TRIM)

Q. What are 3 benefits of prestorage leukocyte reduction vs bedside

  1. Reduces leukocytes before they become activated
  2. Better quality control
  3. Avoids rare reactions with bedside filters (hypotensive reactions)

Q. Why is leukocyte reduction not required for FFP and FP24?

●      Because the product is frozen during production so leukocytes are rendered non-functional

Q. What are five well defined indications for irradiated blood?

1.     IUT → Fetuses undergoing intrauterine transfusion

2.     Newborns who have previously undergone intrauterine transfusions

  1. Patients with congenital cellular immunodeficiency

○      Patients with severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID)

○      Di George syndrome

○      Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency

○      Reticular dysgenesis

○      Cell-mediated immune deficiency of unspecified etiology

  1. Selected patients with acquired immunodeficiency.

○      In particular: patients with Hodgkin’s disease or patients treated with purine antagonists such as fludarabine and patients treated with alemtuzumab (anti-CD52) therapy

  1. Hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients

 

Q. Which medications increase the risk of TA-GvHD and require irradiated blood?

Generic Name

Trade Name(s)

Fludarabine

Fludara

Cladribine (2-CDA)

Leustatin

Deoxycoformicin

Pentostatin, Nipent

Alemtuzumab (anti-CD52)

Campath, Lemtrada

Bendamustine

Treakisym, Ribomustin, Levact, Treanda

Clofarabine

Clolar

Anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG)

Rabbit: Thymoglobulin; Horse: Atgam

 

Q. What are 4 identified but not clear indications for irradiated blood?

●      Preterm infants

●      Patients with hematologic malignancies other than those listed in the definite risk category

●      Patients with solid tumours

●      Patients undergoing solid organ transplantation (if only they receive Alemtuzumab conditioning regimen)

Q. What are two unusual scenarios requiring irradiation?

●      The donor is a blood relative of recipient (directed donation)

●      The donor is selected for HLA compatibility (HLA matched donations)

●      Granulocyte transfusions

Q. Why do we irradiated cellular blood products?

●      To prevent TA-GVHD

Q. Irradiated blood product function and RBC life span

●      Red cell components may be irradiated up to 28 days after collection.

●      Irradiated cells must be transfused as soon as possible, but no later than 14 days after irradiation, and in any case, no later than 28 days after collection.

●      Does not kill donor lymphocytes, but prevents them from replicating thereby removing risk of TA-GVHD

Q. What are the radiation dose recommendations for blood irradiation?

●      The recommended radiation dose is 25 Gy to the central point of the blood pack with a minimum dose of 15 Gy to other parts, and a maximum dose of 50 Gy

Q. What are the 3 radiation sources to irradiate blood products?

●      Irradiation using a 137Cs, 60Co, or X-ray source is the only effective technique for the prevention of TA-GvHD.

Q. What are the two drawbacks of irradiated red cell units?

●      Shortened shelf life → 28-day shelf life from time of irradiation

●      Increased potassium leakage from erythrocytes.

 

A five year old boy is undergoing allogeneic stem cell transplantation for refractory B-ALL. He is currently day 10 post transplantation. Other than packed RBC, what fresh or frozen blood components which would require irradiation if ordered. What would not require irradiation?

·       Buffy coat platelets, apheresis platelets, granulocytes, any directed donation

·       Frozen plasma, SD plasma, Cryo, pooled platelet psoralen treated, pathogen inactivated apheresis

 

9.Infectious disease in TM

Q. What infectious agents does CBS test donor units for? (8 are tested)

●      Antibodies (serology):

○      HIV-1 and HIV-2

○      HCV virus

○      HTLV 1 and 2

○      Hep B core antigen

○      Hep B surface antigen

○      T cruzi (Chagas) (at risk donors only)

●      Viral RNA (PCR/NAT):

○      HIV-1 (double test)

○      HCV (double test)

○      WNV*

●      Viral DNA (PCR/NAT):

○      Hep B virus (double test)

●      Syphilis and bacterial growth (“Bac-T”)

Q. What organisms are only screened for on history? (ie not tested for)

 

●      COVID-19

●      Malaria

●      Babesiosis

●      Leishmaniasis

●      CJD

●      Zika

●      CMV

Q. What is the sole indication of CMV seronegative transfusion in addition to leukoreduction by NAC?

·       intrauterine transfusion

Q. What organism causes chagas disease?

●      Trypanosoma cruzi

Q. Who is tested for T. cruzi?

●      Donor born in or spent at least six continuous months in Mexico, Central or South America

●      Donor's mother or maternal grandmother, were born in these regions (can be vertical transmission)

●      These donors are tested for Chagas antibody (serology)

Q. Who is tested for West Nile virus?

●      PCR/NAT testing is performed during endemic periods (seasonal)

Q. What is the usual West Nile virus season in Canada?

●      Spring and summer → mid-April to October (source: CBS WNV surveillance)

Q. Where do contaminating organisms in blood transfusion come from?

●      1) Skin of blood donor

●      2) Undetected bacteremia in donor

●      3) Environmental contamination during product processing or manipulation

Q: What measures can reduce the risk of bacterial contamination in blood products?

·       Thorough cleansing of donor's arm before venepuncture

·       Diversion of first 40 ml of donor blood for testing

·       Screening of platelet units for bacteria

·       Pathogen inactivation using chemical or photodynamic decontamination

·       Proper storage and handling of blood products

 

Q. What are 3 most common bacteria in blood transfusion sepsis? (gram positive ones)

●      Staph aureus

●      Staph epidermidis

●      Bacillus cereus

Q. What are 4 most common gram-negative transfusion sepsis bugs?

●      E Coli

●      Klebsiella pneumonia

●      Serratia Marcescens

●      Pseudomonas species

●      Yersinia enterocolitica

●      “SKYPE”

10.QC and equipment in TM

Q. What are the requirements of a blood bank fridge?

●      Clean

●      Well lighted

●      Labelled shelves

●      Fans to circulate air through unit evenly

●      Temperature

○      Recording system that continuously monitors and records temperature.

○      Temperature must be recorded every 4 hours.

○      Two separate thermometers are required.

○      One in a fluid volume smaller than the smallest blood component

●      Alarm → Visual and audible alarm system to notify if storage temperatures are not correct

●      Power → Both the alarm system and the storage units themselves must have separate electrical power systems as well as backup systems in case of power failure

Q. What are the QC intervals for freezers and refrigerators?

●      Temperature

○      Recorder - daily

○      Manual temperature - daily

○      Temperature charts (reviewed daily) - weekly

●      Alarm

○      Alarm system board (if applicable) - daily

○      Alarm activation - quarterly

 

Q. What are the requirements for thermometers in blood bank fridge?

●      Must be 2 thermometers that are in agreement within 2C with one of them at the furthest distance possible from the internal monitoring thermometer.

●      The internal monitoring temperature recording sensor must be in a volume of liquid equal to or less than the smallest volume of blood stored in the refrigerator.

●      Liquid -> water is an acceptable fluid to be in since it is less dense than blood and senses changes faster than blood would

●      Annual calibration: All thermometers should be checked against a certified calibrated thermometer at least annually and the check must be documented (CSTM)

Q. What are the requirements for an audible blood bank fridge alarm?

●      All incubators, fridges and freezers must be connected to an audible alarm

●      Audible alarms must be located in an area that is staffed at all times

●      Audible alarms must be connected to an emergency power supply.

○      The backup system should be checked every 6 months.

○      This check must be documented

●      The alarm activation points shall be set at temperatures that allow for corrective action to be taken prior to the blood components and blood products reaching unacceptable temperatures. 

●      The activation points shall be verified according to the manufacturer’s recommendations or at least annually (CSTM, 3.2.2.3)

Q. Platelet incubators QC requirements?

 

  • Temperature

○      Incubator temperature recorder - daily

○      Incubator manual temperature - daily

○      Incubator temperature charts (review daily) – weekly

  • Alarm → Incubator alarm activation - quarterly

·       Ambient platelet storage - every 4 hours if not stored in controlled temperature equipment.

Q. Centrifuge/cell washers QC requirements?

●      Speed - quarterly

●      Timer - quarterly

●      Function - yearly

●      Tube fill level (serologic) - day of use saline fill volume (serologic) - weekly

●      Volume of AHG dispensed (if applicable) - monthly

●      Temperature check (refrigerated centrifuge) - day of use

●      Temperature verification (refrigerated centrifuge) – monthly

Q. Blood irradiators QC requirements?

●      Calibration - yearly

●      Turntable - yearly

●      Timer - monthly/quarterly

●      Source decay - dependent on radiation source type (material)

●      Leak test - twice yearly

●      Dose delivery check (with indicator) - each use

●      Dose delivery verification - depends on isotope used (cobalt, cesium)

Q. What are the QC intervals on microhematocrit centrifuges?

●      Timer Check – quarterly

●      Calibration - quarterly

●      Packed cell volume – yearly

Q. What is QC interval for heating blocks/waterbaths/view boxes?

●      Temperature - day of use

●      Quadrant check – periodically

Q. Automated gel card screening QC?

●      -MTS card daily for screening cells with anti-Fya

●      -Maintenance twice annually

Q. How often should QC be done on component thawing devices?

●      Day of use

●      Thawing devices-temperature shall be checked and documented with each use.

Q. How often should QC be done on pipettes?

●      Quarterly

●      Verification of adequate volume, reduction of carry-over and absence of contamination shall be checked.

Q. How often should QC be done on sterile docking?

●      Weld check each use.

●      Function should be tested yearly

●      Regular sterility checks of blood components processed with a SCD

Q. How often should QC be done on timers/clocks?

●      Twice yearly

Q. How often should liquid in glass thermometers be QC'd?

●      Yearly

Q. How often should pH meters be QC'd?

●      Day of use

Q. How often should QC be done on blood warmers?

●      Quarterly for effluent temperature, heater temperature, and alarm activation

●      The temperature should be documented at each use

Q. What is the QC for blood group and screening cells?

●      Blood group and screening reagents, QC test daily

●      Forward grouping reagents tested against reverse cells (A1 and B); reverse grouping cells testing with anti-A and anti-B; at least 3+ needed

●      Anti-D against R1r and rr cells daily

Q. What are the AABB requirement for record length of storage - how long do you have to keep your records for?

●      Most random things are 10 years.

●      5 years is retention requirement for a lot of clinical things like orders, transfusion reactions etc.

Q. How long should donor and patient records be kept in transfusion?

●      10 years

Q. How long should specimens from transfused donor units or blood donor recipients be kept?

●      7 days after transfusion

Q. What are the four main roles of the transfusion medicine committee?

 

Multidisciplinary committee of stakeholders that provide oversight of a variety of clinical activities as they pertain to transfusion medicine and patient care in hospital environments.

●      1) Minimize inappropriate use of blood

●      2) Reduce product loss due to outdating and wastage

●      3) Monitor transfusion transmitted infections

●      4) Monitor adverse reactions associated with blood transfusion.

7 roles for the blood transfusion committee from another source. The purpose of the transfusion committee shall be to:

●      Help define blood transfusion policies as appropriate to the local clinical activities

●      Ensure that regular evaluations of blood transfusion practices are conducted

●      Set criteria for the evaluation of ordering practices, usage (including discard of blood and blood components)

●      Administration policies, and the ability of services to meet recipient needs

●      Recommend corrective measures, if necessary

●      Disseminate transfusion medicine information and education

●      Evaluate reports of adverse transfusion events and all transfusion errors within the facility, as well as relevant federal and provincial or territorial reports on adverse transfusion events

●      Review available alternatives to allogeneic blood transfusion and make appropriate
recommendations on their use

11.Daratumumab in transfusion medicine

 

What is anti-CD38 therapy and why is it used?
Anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies (e.g., Daratumumab, Isatuximab) target CD38, which is overexpressed in multiple myeloma. They induce cell death and inhibit tumor growth.

 

How does anti-CD38 therapy interfere with transfusion testing?
It binds weakly to CD38 on RBCs, leading to pan-reactivity in antibody screens, positive DATs, and incompatible IAT crossmatches. It does not interfere with ABO/Rh typing or immediate-spin crossmatch.

 

What are the typical lab findings during anti-CD38 therapy?

  • Antibody screen: pan-reactivity with all cells of equal strength
  • DAT: may be positive (IgG ± C3) or frequently negative
  • Auto-control: often negative
  • No hemolysis typically observed

 

What pre-treatment testing is recommended?

  • Group and Screen
  • DAT and extended phenotype or genotype (especially if recently transfused or DAT positive)
  • Document phenotype/genotype with special messages
  • Confirm Daratumumab effects and prepare a wallet card and patient letter

 

What is the testing approach during treatment?

  • For every specimen, confirm DARA
  • If antibody screen shows consistent pan-reactivity, attribute to anti-CD38
  • If variable reaction strengths or new pattern, send to CBS for alloantibody investigation
  • If DAT is positive, follow SOP
  • Reassess every 3 months or when strength changes significantly

 

How is compatibility testing performed?
Crossmatch with fully phenotypically matched RBCs. If incompatible, obtain a Physician Acceptance Letter.

 

What happens after treatment stops?

  • Daratumumab clears in ~4 months, Isatuximab in ~6 months
  • Continue current testing until interference resolves
  • Once cleared, return to routine testing and remove DARA-related notes from patient file

 

How can the effects of anti-CD38 be mitigated in testing?

  • Treat RBCs with DTT, trypsin, or papain (destroys CD38, but also some antigens like Kell, so you cannot rule out K)
  • Use CD38-negative RBCs (cord blood or ln(Ln))
  • Block CD38 on reagent cells with anti-CD38 F(ab')₂ or anti-IgG
  • Neutralize anti-CD38 in plasma using anti-idiotype antibodies or soluble CD38
  • Most importantly, plan ahead and perform extended typing before therapy starts

 

 

12. Passenger lymphocyte syndrome

Etiology

·       Specific type of graft-versus-host disease resulting in immune-mediated hemolysis in the post-transplant patient

 

Type of ABO mismatch

·       Major: recipient A/B antibodies directed against donor ABO antigens

·       Minor: recipient expresses an ABO antigen not present in the donor allograft

 

Pathogenesis of PLS

·       In minor ABO mismatched allograft, stimulated donor B-lymphocytes produce antibodies present in recipient RBC after transplant

·       Hemolysis due to complement-mediated RBC destruction

 

Clinical manifestation

·       Present 1-3 weeks post-transplant

·       Typically mild and self-limiting

 

Treatment

·       Most treated by transfusion of blood products

·       PRBC match donor ABC type (ie. Donor B and recipient AB, transfuse either B or O type PRBC)

·       Plasma match recipient ABO type

1.Transfusion reactions

 

a.Work up

 

What is your approach if a patient has a transfusion reaction - what are the immediate steps to take (6)?

 

  1. Stop the transfusion
  2. Maintain IV access
  3. Check vital signs (ABCs, IV, O2, monitors, full set of vitals)
  4. Clerical checks
    1. Patient ID (wrist band)
    2. Sample ID/product label
  5. Notify physician → physician should assess the patient
  6. Notify blood bank
    1. Complete appropriate paperwork
    2. Send appropriate samples

 

When are patients monitored during a transfusion reaction (4)?

 

●      Vitals should be taken at the following points during transfusion:

○      Before (baseline) transfusion

○      After 15 mins transfusion (slow initial rate)

○      At the completion transfusion

○      At any point during transfusion if there is concern about a transfusion reaction

 

When should the patient be monitored aside from vitals?

 

●      Every hour

●      Final set of observations 15 mins after the unit is transfused

 

When can you continue a transfusion reaction? What are the 2 possible scenarios when you might do this?

 

  1. Minor allergic reaction (rash/hives/pruritus)
    1. Urticaria, rash or itching involving < 2/3rd of body
    2. No other symptoms
    3. If it doesn’t improve within 30 mins, you would stop
  2. FNHTR
    1. Toronto: Temp of 38 to 38.9 with no other symptoms
    2. Blood Easy: >1 degree rise in temp AND >38 degrees during or up to 4 hrs post transfusion

 

Note: institutional policies may vary

Most people are in agreement that you can safely continue in the above 2 scenarios

 

 

What are the 4 basic elements of transfusion testing? (eg., if a reaction occurred)

 

  1. Clerical check
  2. Visual inspection for hemolysis
  3. ABO check
  4. DAT

 

What are 3 methods for measuring free Hb?

 

  1. Visual inspection of plasma after centrifugation
  2. Mass spec with plasma sample
  3. Peroxidase reaction (causes a measurable colour change that can be measured)
  4. Direct spectrophotometric method measuring free Hb in plasma (540 nm). Can measure free Hb directly in plasma

 

What is the sensitivity of a post TF blood sample inspection for Hemoglobinemia?

 

●      Visual inspection can detect as little as 2.5 ml of hemolyzed blood

●      Centrifuge and look for a colour change in the plasma, sensitive to low levels of hemolysis - as little as 2.5 ml, quick & easy but not specific

 

What are the 3 different Tiers of Transfusion Reaction testing?

 

●      Tier 1 → STOP the transfusion, maintain IV access then x 4 things done immediately:

○      1) Clerical check (right pt & right product)

○      2) Draw post TF blood sample for Hemoglobinemia

○      3) DAT (remember to compare with pre-transfusion DAT as 20% are incidentally positive)

○      4) Repeat ABO (if you identify a problem, consider the “companion error” - who is the other patient getting the wrong blood?)

●      Tier 2 → essentially, hemolysis screen

○      Done if anything in tier 1 raises suspicion of hemolysis

○      Smear, bili, LDH, hapto, urine Hb (can dipstick for this)

○      Coags

○      Renal function & electrolytes

○      ABO type and DAT on unit as well as pre and post transfusion samples

○      Repeat the AHG crossmatch and antibody screen using pre and post transfusion samples - may want to switch method for IAT, tubes if solid phase previously and potentially use LISS

●      Tier 3 → Antibody Investigation (phenotype donor unit & pre-transfusion sample)

○      Eluate (pre and post samples) → see if there is an antibody present

○      Antibody Investigation on donor units, Investigate transfusion technique and blood component storage conditions

○      Could phenotype unit

○      Order additional investigations (lactate, coags etc to evaluate for DIC etc)

●      Concept of tiers compartmentalizes your approach/answer → demonstrate a logical organized approach

●      See BB Guy for discussion of this concept

In what circumstances do you have to report a transfusion reaction within 24 hrs to CBS

●      BACON

Definition

●      HTN

●      Consider a single unit transfusion

What is the management of TACO?
