d.TRALI

2004 Canadian Consensus Conference Panel TRALI and Acute Lung Injury (ALI) definitions

 

What is the definition of TRALI? (new definition with TRALI Type 1 and 2)

 

  • Acute lung injury (defined below) occurring within 6 hours of completion of transfusion of blood product.
  • No pre-existing acute lung injury.
  • No other temporally-associated risk factors for acute lung injury (Table 1).

TRALI type 1
  • Acute onset (within 6 hours of transfusion)
  • Hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 ≤ 300 or SpO2 < 90% on room air)
  • Clear evidence of bilateral pulmonary edema on imaging (CXR, chest computed tomography (CT), or ultrasound)
  • No evidence of left atrial hypertension (LAH) or, if LAH is present, it is not the main contributor to the hypoxemia
  • No temporal relationship to an alternative risk factor for ARDS

TRALI type 2
  • Same clinical criteria as TRALI Type I (see first four bullets defining TRALI type 1 above)
  • Presence of an ARDS risk factor or mild ARDS (P/F 200-300)
  • Previously stable pulmonary status in the 12 hours prior to transfusion

 

What is Possible TRALI?

 

  • Acute lung injury (defined below) occurring within 6 hours of transfusion.
  • No pre-existing acute lung injury.
  • One or more temporally-associated risk factors for acute lung injury.

 

What is the definition of Acute Lung Injury?

●       New onset.

●       Hypoxemia SpO2 <90% or Pa02/Fi02 < 300 mm Hg on room air, or other clinical evidence of hypoxemia.

●       Bilateral infiltrates on frontal chest X-ray

No evidence of circulatory overload (Transfusion associated circulatory overload includes any four of the following occurring within 6 h of a BT[3] - acute respiratory distress, tachycardia, increased blood pressure (BP), acute or worsening pulmonary edema and evidence of a positive fluid balance.)

 

What are the Berlin definition of risk factors for ARDS?

Direct Lung Injury

Indirect Lung Injury

Aspiration of gastric contents
Pneumonia
Inhalation injury
Pulmonary contusion
Pulmonary vasculitis
Drowning

Non-pulmonary sepsis
Major trauma
Severe burns
Pancreatitis
Noncardiogenic shock
Drug overdose

 

 

What is the etiology/pathophysiology of TRALI (2)?

-        according to BE5, 1. Antibody mediated theory, 2. Neutrophils priming hypothesis (see below product)

●      1) Patient: Adherence of neutrophils to lung endothelium

○      Risk factors

■      Sepsis

■      Mechanical ventilation

■      Increased time on CPB

■      Heme malignancy

■      Bleeding in liver failure

■      Massive transfusion

■      Positive fluid balance

●      2) Product

○      Antibody mediated

■      HLA or HNA antibodies from donor product

■      Multiparous female with plasma product

○      Pro-inflammatory mediators

■      Bioactive lipids from donor product

■      Other ligands sCD40L

■      Storage/age

Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) | Professional Education (blood.ca)

TRALI is thought to result from two distinct clinical events, often referred to as the "two-hit hypothesis":

  1. First Event (Recipient Condition):
    • The patient has a predisposing condition that primes neutrophils. This can be due to active infection, recent surgery, cytokine therapy, trauma (e.g., severe burns), or other inflammatory conditions.
    • This leads to activation of the pulmonary endothelium, causing primed neutrophils to sequester (accumulate) in the lungs.
  2. Second Event (Transfusion):
    • The transfusion introduces donor-derived antibodies (e.g., anti-HLA or anti-HNA antibodies) or biological response modifiers that target the recipient’s neutrophils.
    • These factors activate the primed neutrophils, leading to neutrophil-mediated damage to the pulmonary endothelium and capillaries, causing capillary leak and subsequent pulmonary edema (fluid accumulation in the lungs).

Types of TRALI:

  • Immune TRALI:
    • The more common form, seen in 80-85% of cases, where donor-derived antibodies (anti-HLA/HNA) directly activate the recipient's neutrophils.
  • Non-immune TRALI:
    • Occurs when biological response modifiers (e.g., cytokines, lipids) present in the transfused blood trigger neutrophil activation, even in the absence of donor antibodies.

Threshold Hypothesis:

  • In cases where the second event (transfusion) is very strong, TRALI can occur even without the first event, meaning it can affect patients without prior risk factors.

 

Presentation of TRALI?

 

●      Onset during or within 6 hours of a transfusion

●      Rapid onset of dyspnea and tachypnea

●      Oxygen saturation <90% on room air (hypoxia)

●      Fever, cyanosis and hypotension

●      CXR bilateral non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, bilateral pathy infiltrates

●      No signs of left atrial hypertension

●      Low BNP

●      Transient leukopenia

 

Natural history of TRALI & Treatment?

 

●      Natural History

○      Resolves in 24-72 hours

○      72% require mechanical ventilation

○      5-10% fatality

●      Treatment

○      Supportive care

■      Mechanical ventilation

○      Diuretics/Steroids not useful

 

What are some differentiating features between TRALI and TACO?

●      TRALI

○      More severe hypoxia

○      Hypotension

○      Fever

○      Leukopenia/thrombocytopenia transiently

○      CXR diffuse bilateral infiltrates, no evidence of circulatory overload

○      Within 6 hours of transfusion

○      No response to diuretic

●      TACO

○      Hypertension

○      No fever

○      BNP increased (can be in TRALI as well apparently)

○      CXR diffuse bilateral infiltrates with circulatory overload

○      During or immediately after a transfusion

○      Respond to diuretic

 

What are the TRALI-mitigating measures that CBS has implemented

●      Primary Prevention Measures for TRALI

○      Male donors for transfusable plasma

○      Male donors for platelet apheresis

○      Male plasma for platelet pool resuspension

○      Female plasma goes for fractionation!

○      RBC plasma volume less than 7.5 mL in B1, B2 = 18mL

○      Future:

■      Solvent detergent plasma

■      Pathogen inactivation

What is the CBS follow-up for TRALI?

●      Secondary Prevention

○      Investigate reported TRALIs

■      CBS TRALI medical review group

○      Test donors associated with TRALI/ Possible TRALI

○      Test for HLA antibody but not anti-HNA (no easily available assay)

○      Defer implicated donors (HLA antibody positive)

○      Restrict HLA antibody-negative donors to plasma for fractionation

●      Testing:

○      Patient sample to CBS

●      CBS follow-up

○      Staff will likely call you/staff to discuss

○      If assessed as TRALI or possible TRALI

■      All in-date transfusable companion products collected within 12 months of reaction

■      Temporary 3 months deferral to all associated donors

■      CBS notifies donor

○      Clinical information needed because

■      TRALI assessment for TRALI Medical Review Group

■      Affects disposition of donors

■      Results of preliminary report needs to occur within 15 days

○      Donors:

■      If not considered TRALI, possible TRALI, or inconclusive,

■      Donor is flagged, and deferred if they have 2 flags!

■      If considered TRALI, possible TRALI or inconclusive

■      Donor is tested for HLA-antibodies

■      If no antibodies, then can continue to donate, but plasma goes to fractionation

■      If antibodies, then cannot give again!

Incidence of TRALI with plasma, PLTs & RBCs?

 

●      Rough #s provided by Jason

○      1 in 1,200 - 5000 for plasma and PLTs

○      1 in 5000 for RBCs

○      1 in 10,000 by BE5 but seems higher in real life

 

List two transfusion complications related to HLA antibodies and two related to HPA antibodies.

-        TRALI due to class I and II HLA-Ab

-        Platelet refractoriness due to class I HLA-Ab

-        Platelet refractoriness due to HPA-Ab

-        PTP due to anti-HPA-1a

e.AHTR

 

What is AHTR?

 

●      Acute hemolysis from pre-formed antibodies in patient (usually ABO)

●      Naturally occurring AB’s

 

What are other causes of hemolysis during a transfusion (ie. non-immune mediated)

 

●      Hemolyzed unit

●      Faulty blood warmer

●      Small bore IV/ high transfusion rates

●      Infused with incompatible fluid (ie. anything other than 0.9% Normal saline and 5% albumin)

 

What are the signs and symptoms of AHTR?

●      Symptoms

○      Chills

○      apprehension

○      agitation

○      pain at IV site

○      Flushing

○      chest pain

○      SOB

○      Nausea

●      Signs

○      Fever

○      Hypotension

○      hemoglobinuria

○      collapse

○      vomiting

○      bleeding from puncture sites (ie. DIC within hours)

●      Usually within minutes! Ie really acute!

●      Markers: increased bilirubin, increased LDH, increased AST>ALT, decreased haptoglobin

What is the death rate of AHTR?

●      <10% result in death

What are the steps to manage an ATR?

●      Stop the transfusion

●      Maintain IV access

●      Check vital signs

●      Clerical checks

○      Patient ID

○      Sample ID/product label

●      Notify physician → physician should assess the patient

●      Notify blood bank

○      Complete appropriate paperwork

○      Send appropriate samples for AHTR w/u

●      IV fluids and vasopressor support

●      Mannitol or furosemide to maintain renal blood flow

●      Identify and treat DIC supportively if present

 

What is an important consideration in AHTR?

●      CONSIDER OTHER PATIENTS!!!

●      Who got the other product?!

●      Is there another patient at risk?

What is the cause of ABO-related AHTR?

●      Almost always due to human error

○      Sample collection (wrong blood in tube) (15%)

○      Sample transfusion (incorrect blood component transfused) (majority)

○      Rarely at TMS lab error

○      Rarely product labelling/CBS

f.Allergic reactions

 

What are Allergic reactions in Transfusion?

●      Mild: Hives, Urticaria, Rash

●      Severe: Facial/airway edema, bronchospasm, wheeze, GI symptoms

When do allergic reactions usually occur?

●      Onset usually within first hour

What are the causes of allergic transfusion reactions?

●      Most are unexplained

○      Recipient has IgE antibody to a donor Ag

○      Passive transfusion of antigen eg peanut or other protein to a sensitized recipient

○      Or other way: Donor has IgE against recipient protein

○      IgA or haptoglobin deficient patient

■      Although most not at risk of anaphylactic reaction

■      1 in 500 donors are IgA deficient, 1 in 1,500 donors have anti-IgA, not clear risk to cause anaphylactic transfusion reaction

Minor allergic reaction – urticaria

·       Clinical presentation: one urticarial lesion to widespread urticarial lesions

·       May have pruritic, erythema, flushing, mild upper respiratory symptoms, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea

·       Interrupt the transfusion, give diphenhydramine 25-50 mg po or iv

What is a hypotensive transfusion reaction?  What products is it associated with? And what is the Ddx?

●      Drop in Systolic BP of >30 mm Hg AND drop has to be less than 80 mm Hg SBP

●      ACE inhibitor +/- bedside leukoreduction filter (ACE responsible for bradykinin degradation) (50% on ACEi)

●      Bradykinin-associated

○      vasoactive peptide

●      Can be associated with in-line filters, or the regular leukoreduction filters from CBS

●      Products

○      Platelets > than other products

○      Allo/auto RBCs implicated

●      DDx:

○      TRALI, AHTR/Hemolysis, Anaphylaxis, Bacterial contamination

What are the Risk Factors for hypotensive transfusion reaction?

(from TM Exam 2018)

○      Leukoreduction filter at beside

○      Leukoreduced product

○      Any negatively charged filter

○      Rapid infusion

○      Blood warmer

○      Prostate surgery

○      Genetic polymorphism leading to decreased bradykinin degradation

g.DHTR

What is the cause of DHTR?

●      DHTR: Anamnestic alloantibody production

○      Pre-transfusion titer is absent or too low to detect (neg screen)

○      Memory B cells are primed to recognize cognate foreign antigen

○      Commonly implicated antigens: E, Jka, c, Fya, K

When do DHTR occur?

●      Technically any reaction after 24 hours to 28 days (endpoint)

●      Generally 7-14 days post transfusion

●      Rare primary immune response with extra-vascular hemolysis

What are the S&S of DHTR?

●      Symptoms/signs

○      Unexpected anemia

○      Jaundice

●      Asymptomatic

What is the workup of DHTR?

●      Workup

○      CBC + retic

○      LDH, bili, blood film review

●      TMS investigation

○      Antibody screen repeat

○      New DAT (mixed field)

○      Can do DAT eluate

○      Antibody investigation

●      Try to avoid further transfusion until figured it out

○      But if they need it, give it!

What are prevention strategies for DHTR?

●      Prevention

○      Prophylactic antigen matching

■      Sickle cell anemia

●      Phenotype or genotype early

●      Prophylactic match for: Rh (D, C, c, E, e) and Kell

●      If allo antibodies formed, additionally match for Kidd, Duffy (Fya) and S, s plus give antigen negative for their antibodies

■      WAIHA

○      Thalassemia, MDS

What is a Delayed serologic transfusion reaction? How does it differ from a delayed HTR?

●      Similar to DHTR, but the patient doesn’t have hemolysis → just serological conversion

○      ie. just a new positive antibody screen with a new alloantibody

○      Serological evidence of incompatibility but no hemolysis

What is Hyperhemolysis?

●      Acute and delayed (<7 days, >7 days)

●      Pathophysiology poorly understood

○      Both autologous and donor red cells destroyed

○      Theories

■      Bystander hemolysis

■      Complement activation

■      Suppression of erythropoiesis (classically reticulocytopenia)

■      Macrophage activation

●      Mild/severe

●      RBC transfusion may exacerbate

○      Try not to transfuse

●      DAT is neg with early (< 7 days) but pos with delayed (> 7 days)

●      New allo ab seen with delayed (> 7 days)

4 patient groups at risk of hyperhemolysis?

●      Most commonly in HbSS

●      Also possible in PMF, ACD, Thal

 

h.TA-GVHD (cytopenias after transfusion)

A systematic review of transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease | Blood | American Society of Hematology (ashpublications.org)

 

What is the cause of TA-GVHD? Explain the “setup” for TA-GVHD

 

●      Cause → viable lymphocytes in a transfused blood product attack an immunosuppressed host or occurs with a haploidentical match which causes subsequent immune tolerance in the recipient and destruction of the recipient cells by the donor lymphocytes

●      Setup

○      1) Viable lymphocytes in donor product (hence benefit of irradiation)

○      2) Recipient immunodeficiency OR recipient heterozygous and donor homozygous at a given HLA site

 

Explain the concept of being “haploidentical” in the pathophysiology of TA-GVHD?

 

Uniformly fatal Transfusion reaction due to homozygous donor for alleles that are haploidentical to recipient

●      Recipient doesn’t recognize the donor as foreign

●      Donor lymphocytes engraft and attack recipient

 

 

Who is at risk for TA-GVHD?

●      At risk:

○      T cell dysfunction

○      Lymphopenia

○      Directed donation

○      HLA-matched product

○      Walking donor

○      Populations with limited HLA diversity (Japan)

○      Granulocyte transfusion

●      Indications for irradiated red blood cells (RBCs) and platelets

○      Intrauterine transfusion

○      Neonatal exchange transfusion*

○      Congenital cell-mediated immunodeficiencies*

○      Hodgkin lymphoma (not time-limited; applies to all transfusions during the patient's lifetime)

○      Hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients (autologous or allogeneic)

○      Donors of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cells (only applies to the week prior to and during stem cell harvest)

○      CAR-T therapy recipients (applies 7 days prior to collection and 3 months post-infusion)

○      Purine analog therapy for any diagnosis (eg, fludarabine, cladribine, deoxycoformycin, bendamustine, clofarabine)

○      ATG or alemtuzumab therapy for hematologic disease (but not for other diagnoses)

○      Recipients of donations from biologic relatives

○      Recipients of donations selected on the basis of HLA matching

 

What is the clinical presentation of TA-GVHD?

●      Presents:

○      Delayed reaction (because donor lymphocytes engraftment)

○      8-14 (median 11) days from the implicated transfusion

○      Rash 80%, fever 67%, liver enzyme elevation 66%, pancytopenia 65%, diarrhea 43%, bone marrow aplasia 23%, hepatomegaly 14% (multisystem failure)

○      Mortality rate > 90%

○      Rare- only 0.1% - 1% of at risk patients

 

What are the implicated components?

●      RBC 38%, whole blood 26%, platelet 6%

 

What are the treatments for TA-GVHD?

●      Immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory medications

 

What is Post-transfusion purpura?

●      Patient has antibody to platelet antigen (anti-HPA1a) in the transfused product (RBC, plasma, platelets)

●      5-10 days post transfusion

○      Profound thrombocytopenia

○      Purpura/bleeding

○      Self-limited

○      Recovery in 7-48 hours

●      Not well understood why they destroy their own platelets too

○      ie. similar to Hyperhemolysis

●      An alloantibody that behaves like an autoantibody

●      8% mortality, death from ICH

●      PTP should be considered when a platelet refractory patient fails to respond to HLA-matched platelets

 

What is the most common HPA antigen associated with PTP?

●      Most common HPA 1a

○      Rarely Anti-HLA

○      Same as NAIT

 

What are the most common Gram positive bacterial infections from transfusion?

 

  1. Staphylococcus aureus
  2. Staphylococcus epidermidis
  3. Bacillus cereus

 

What are the most common Gram negative bacterial infections from transfusion?

 

  1. Serratia marcescens
  2. Klebsiella pneumonia
  3. Yersinia enterocolitica
  4. Pseudomonas species
  5. Escherichia coli

 

“SKYPE” - Genius!!

 

Where do the organisms come from in septic transfusion reactions - give 3 egs?

 

  1. Undiagnosed bacteremia in donor
  2. Donor skin at the time of collection
  3. During product manipulation and processing

j.Transfusion reaction reporting

1. Definition of ATR

An Adverse Transfusion Reaction (ATR) is an unintended and undesirable response to blood components or plasma protein products, deemed definitely, probably, or possibly related to the transfusion.

2. National Hemovigilance Framework

  • TTISS (Transfusion Transmitted Injuries Surveillance System) is Canada's national hemovigilance system, coordinated by the Public Health Agency of Canada.
  • In Ontario, TTISS-ON is coordinated by the McMaster Centre for Transfusion Research.
  • Data are de-identified and aggregated for national monitoring.

3. Reporting Pathways and Stakeholders

Entity

Reportable To

TTISS-ON

All serious ATRs (excluding minor allergic, febrile non-hemolytic, delayed serologic). Submit via REDCap database or fax using CTAERF.

Canadian Blood Services (CBS)

ATRs due to suspected blood component quality/safety issues or CBS errors (e.g. bacterial contamination, mislabelling).

Health Canada – Canada Vigilance Program

Required under Blood Regulations and Vanessa’s Law. Serious/fatal ATRs reported within 24h; others within 15 days.

Manufacturer of Plasma Derivatives

All ATRs (serious and minor clusters) related to plasma protein products (PPP), such as IVIg, factor concentrates, etc.

Form used: Canadian Transfusion Adverse Event Reporting Form (CTAERF). Must exclude patient name and OHIP number for fax/email.

4. Key Reaction Types and Examples

Reaction Type

Reporting Notes

Severe Allergic / Anaphylaxis

TTISS-ON + CBS + Health Canada

TRALI / Possible TRALI

TTISS-ON + CBS + Health Canada

Bacterial / Viral contamination

TTISS-ON + CBS + Health Canada

Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO)

TTISS-ON (esp. if related to bedside error or device)

Minor Allergic / FNHTR

TTISS-ON only (unless in clusters → Health Canada under Vanessa’s Law)

Plasma Derivative–related reactions

Report to Manufacturer + TTISS-ON + Health Canada if serious

5. Vanessa’s Law (Effective Dec 2019)

  • Mandatory reporting of serious ATRs from Plasma Protein Products (PPP) by hospitals to Health Canada.
  • Acceptable to use TTISS form if it includes required fields (e.g., patient age, drug info, outcome).
  • Minor ATRs only need to be reported if appearing in clusters.

6. Ontario’s Sentinel Site Model

  • 29 hospitals voluntarily report all ATRs, including minor ones, forming a provincial surveillance network.
  • These hospitals represent ~35% of blood use in Ontario.
  • Data from these hospitals is used to calculate reaction incidence per blood component type.

7. Hospital Responsibilities

  • Transfusion Services: Investigate, classify, and report ATRs using CTAERF.
  • Prescribers & Nurses: Must recognize and report suspected reactions.
  • Quality & Transfusion Committees: Review reports and educate clinical staff.
  • During site visits, ORBCoN and CBS provide hospital-specific ATR incidence data to support quality improvement.

8. Reporting Deadlines

Condition

Deadline

Fatal ATR (Health Canada)

Within 24 hours

Serious Non-fatal ATR

Within 15 days (Health Canada)

TTISS-ON Reports

Within 3 months (Ontario)

Monthly Updates

Plasma derivative ATRs to TTISS-ON

 

2.Clinically significant antibodies

 

What are clinically significant antibodies?

 

●      Antibodies that are capable of causing hemolysis at 37C OR HDFN

 

What are the general properties of clinically significant antibodies?

 

●      Most are IgG antibodies

○      IgG antibodies react at or near 37 C

○      IgG antibodies are transported across the placenta into the fetal circulation,

●      IgM Antibodies

○      ABO IgM are clinically significant!

○      However, this does NOT mean that all IgM antibodies are insignificant!

 

List the clinically significant Antigens?

●      ABO

●      Rh: DCcEe

●      Kell: K, k

●      Duffy: Fya, Fyb

●      Kidd: Jka, Jkb

○      Mild/uncommon HDFN

●      S/s (+/-U)

 

What are the antigens that are possibly significant when reactive at 37C?

●      Lewis

●      M,N

●      P1

●      Lutheran

●      A1

 

What are additional antibodies that are sometimes clinically significant?

●      Yta

●      Vel

●      Ge

●      Gya

●      Hy

●      Sda

 

What antibodies don’t respect?

●      Lewis

●      N?

●      If only cold-reacting:

○      A1, P1

 

What are the High Titre Low Avidity antibodies - give 5 egs?

●      Antibodies with “high titer, low avidity” (HTLA) features (weakly binding/reacting)

●      High frequency antigens that are generally clinically benign (no HTRs or HDN)

○      Chido, Rodgers most frequent

○      1) Complement components (C4)

○      1) Knops (Kna), McCoy (McCa), JMH

■      (Mnemonic: John Milton Hagen is “knops/not” the real McCoy)

○      Must be careful, because some antibodies with similar features may be significant (anti-Vel, anti-Yta)

3.Rhogam dosing, Indications, Kleihauer-Betke (DISCUSSED IN PEDS!)

4.HDFN Hemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn (HDFN)

a. Requirements

a. The “RAT” model

●      1) Response

○      a) Body responds to foreign antigen by making antibody.

●      2) Access

○      a) Antibody formed must be able to cross placenta.

○      b) IgG1, IgG3, IgG4 cross, IgG2 and IgM do not.

●      3) Target

○      a) Target antigen must be present on fetal RBCs.

b. Manifestations

a. Lab findings

●      1) Anemia

●      2) Indirect hyperbilirubinemia/jaundice

●      3) Positive DAT (unless all cells destroyed - one of the causes of a false neg DAT))

b. “Erythroblastosis fetalis”

●      1) Abundant nucleated RBCs in circulation in response to accelerated destruction

c. Hydrops fetalis

●      1) Most severe form of HDFN, often fatal in utero

●      2) EMH in liver may be so severe as to impair albumin synthesis, leading to volume overload and high-output heart failure → hydrops

 

How do antibodies cross the placenta?

 

Active Trans-placental antibody transfer

●      IgG binds to Fc receptor on the placenta

○      Function is to provide immunity to fetus

●      IgG1>IgG3>IgG2

●      Transfer is active and unidirectional

●      Transfer is slow until 24 weeks

○      Increased until Fetal IgG1>maternal

●      Post-natal T1/2 of IgG is 2-3 weeks

○      Due to baby growth - this is faster than catabolism alone!!

 

What are factors affecting HDFN?

 

●      IgG class

●      Ag specificity

●      Antibody Titre

●      Ab glycosylation

●      Antigen expression level in the neonate

○      Gestational age

○      Erythroid stage

○      Individual variation

●      ABO-incompatibility

○      Mitigates the risk of immunization of the mom, as the RBCs don’t stay around long enough!

Antibodies that can cause HDFN

·       Kidd

·       Rh – D, c

·       Kell - K

·       Duffy

·       Lub (mild)

·       Tja (very significant)

·       Ss

·       U

·       Dia and Dib

·       Wra

What are the most severe types of HDFN?

 

●      Anti-D

●      Anti-c

●      Anti-Kell

●      Others:

○      C,e,E,Fya,Jka

○      ABO! (this is usually mild, not severe)

 

 

What is done in Canada to mitigate HDFN risk?

 

●      Lab tests

○      ABO & Rh

■      +/- RHD genotype

○      Antibody screen

■      If positive:

■      Antibody ID, titration

■      Genotype phenotyping

■      Fetal Red cell antigen genotype

●      Timing

○      First prenatal visit: 6-12 weeks ABO, Rh + screen

■      If antibodies, titration every 4 weeks, then 2 weeks

○      24-26 weeks

■      Repeat ABO Rh and screen in all Rh negative moms

■      Other countries will repeat the antibody screen at this time as well

■      May do previously transfused or multiparous mothers at this time!

■      Sample from father is requested if mother has clinically significant antibody

○      28 weeks

■      Routine RhIG for eligible patients

○      40 weeks

■      Post-natal cord testing - and antigen type

■      FMH screen and RhIG if required

What is the NAC position on Weak D?

 

●      Prenatal patients with discrepant, weak or inconclusive serological RhD
test results should be further investigated with RHD genotyping to determine RhIg candidacy and optimal Rh type for transfusion.

 

What is the most common type of HDFN?

 

●      ABO HDFN (for mild hemolysis)

●      Anti D, c, K for severe HDFN

 

c. ABO HDFN

 

Why is ABO HDFN mild/undiagnosed?

 

●      1) Weak ABO antigen expression in utero

●      2) Soluble plasma ABO antigens neutralize antibodies

 

When does ABO HDFN affect pregnancies?

 

●      Present in first (or any) pregnancy

●      Group O moms, group A or B babies

 

What is the testing for ABO HDFN?

 

Lab testing

●      Baby ABO, Rh, Ab screen on baby or mom sample

●      Cord blood DAT +/-

○      a) Coated cells might be destroyed, or:

○      b) Cells may be very weakly coated

●      Antibody screen neg. (screen cells are group O)

●      Eluate from fetal cells + with A and/or B cells

 

What is the treatment for ABO HDFN?

 

●      No intervention is usually necessary

●      If severe, treat as outlined under Rh section below.

 

d. Rh HDFN/RhIg

List three explanations for a finding of anti-D antibody in a patient who types as Rh positive. (SMH)

-        Partial D

-        Weak D

-        Lab error

-        Alternative: partial D, autoantibody with D specificity, passive anti-D (RhIG)

 

Who gets RH HDFN?

 

●      Not first pregnancy (unless mom was transfused)

●       D-neg moms, D+ babies

 

What mitigates Rh HDFN?

 

●      ABO incompatibility reduces likelihood

 

What does the initial neonatal lab testing show in Rh HDFN? (Blood group, DAT, Antibody screen, Eluate, Bili)

 

●      Infant D+ (unless “blocked D”)

○      a) “Blocked D”= false negative D antigen test due to excessive coating of D+ cells with anti-D

●      DAT strongly positive

●      Antibody screen: anti-D

●      Eluate: anti-D

●      Indirect bilirubin elevated

●      Increased change in amniotic fluid optical density at 450 nm (Liley/Queenan graph)

 

What is the treatment for Rh HDFN?

 

●      Keep bilirubin < 20

○      Lower threshold in premature babies

○      Indirect bilirubin can cross the blood/brain barrier and cause kernicterus (basal ganglia and brainstem bilirubin deposition).

●      Phototherapy

●      Exchange transfusion with D- blood as necessary

 

How do you prevent HDFN from Rh?

 

●      RhIG: commercially prepared anti-D

 

 

What are the two types of RhIg available?

 

●      “RhoGam”, “BayRho-D”: IM forms

●      “WinRho”, “Rhophylac”: IV or IM forms

 

What is the mechanism of RhIg?

 

●      Prevents D antigen recognition in vulnerable mom

 

What are the 3 indications for RhIg?

 

●      Obstetric indications

○      D-neg female at about 28 weeks gestation

○      D-neg female < 72 hours of D+ infant’s birth

○      D-neg female with pregnancy complications or invasive procedures (amnio, cordocentesis)

 

When do you give RhIg?

 

●      If Rh negative with no Anti-D at first prenatal

○      Repeat screen and administer RhIg at 28 weeks gestation

○      Repeat testing in Rh positive mothers is controversial

●      If Rh negative or unknown, cord testing should be performed at delivery

○      RhIg administered to all D negative women who deliver a D positive baby

○      Maternal antibody screen positive for Anti D

■      Could it be passive anti D from previous RhIg?

●      Always err on the side of more RhIg if passive vs. immune uncertain!

●      Also indicated for RhD negative women without Anti-D and:

○      Antepartum hemorrhage

○      Spontaneous/therapeutic abortion

○      Threatened abortion

○      Ectopic pregnancy

○      IUFD and stillbirth

○      In-utero therapeutic interventions

○      Abdominal trauma

○      Obstetrical manipulations

○      Amnio/CVS/cordocentesis

○      Molar pregnancy

○      Transfusion of D+ blood components

■      ie. platelets!

 

What is the risk of RhD immunization by platelet component?

 

●      1%

 

What are the contraindications for RhIg?

 

●      D-negative pregnant female who has already made her own anti-D

○      Think about prior RhIg, especially on exams

○      RhIg has a 25-day half-life, but may be detectable for as long as six months

○      Usually distinguishable from maternal anti-D by weak reactions

■      IgM component, and low titer (almost always < 4)

●      D+ females

●      D-neg mom, D-neg baby (no postpartum dose)

 

How much fetal blood (or red blood cells) does RhIg cover?

 

●      One full dose vial (300 ug or 1500 IU) per 30 ml of D+ whole blood (15 ml D+ RBCs)

○      “Mini-dose” (50 ug) sometimes used after 1st trimester abortion for < 5 ml whole blood

 

What is the half life of RhIg?

 

●      21-24 days

 

What are the RHIG doses used for pregnancy complications? Bloody easy 4

●      <12 weeks → 120 ug IV/IM

●      12-20 weeks → 300 ug IV/IM

●      >20 weeks → 300ug + FMH assessment to determine if additional doses required.

 

Name the qualitative and quantitative tests for Maternal Fetal hemorrhage testing.

 

●      Qualitative:

○      Rosette test

●      Quantitative

○      Kleihauer Betke

○      Flow Cytometry

 

 

What is the Kleihauer Betke test? What is the principle? (See more below)

 

●      Kleihauer-Betke

○      Quantitative (but poorly reproducible)

○      Acid-resistant Hgb F RBCs stain brightly on blood smear

○      Result is a percentage (% of mom’s blood made of baby blood)

 

What is the purpose of flow cytometry for Maternal Fetal Hemorrhage (see more below)

 

●      Flow cytometry

○      Used in some centers rather than KB

○      Samples many more cells and is considered more accurate

 

How do you use quantitative results of FMH testing?

 

●      Using quant. results (Tech Manual Method)

○      i) KB% x blood volume = baby blood in mom

■      Use 5000 ml if no maternal weight given.

■      If weight given, multiply weight x 70 ml/Kg

○      ii) Baby blood vol/30 = vials of RhIg needed

■      Remember, one vial per 30 ml D+ blood

■      Or if you’ve used HCT to calculate maternal RBC mass, one vial per 15mls fetal RBCs

○      iii) Rounding rules

■      If number after decimal is < 5, round up

■      If > 5, round up twice

■      So, “3.4” would mean give 4 vials, while “3.5” would mean to give 5 vials

○      iv) Example: D– mom with D+ baby. KB=2%

■      0.02 x 5000 = 100 ml D+ baby blood

■      100/30 = 3.33

■      Round up once; give 4 vials

●      An easier and equally accurate way!

○      i) KB% x 5/3 = number of vials

○      ii) In above example, (2 x 5)/3 = 3.33

○      iii) Note: “5” is mom’s BV in L; use whatever number is appropriate

●      Compatibility testing for babies with Rh HDFN

○      1) Mom’s serum may be used to crossmatch.

 

e. Anti-K HDFN

What is unique about HDFN due to Anti-K

 

●      Relatively common; particularly severe

●      Anti-K attaches to K antigen on early RBC precursors and causes severe fetal anemia

●      Less hemolysis than other forms of HDFN (less hyperbilirubinemia and reticulocytosis)

Rosette Test

When is the rosette test positive? How is it performed?

●      Rosette Test - positive when 5mL of Rh positive RBCs are present

○      Incubate a maternal 3-5% red cell suspension with IgG anti-D at 37°C. The anti-D will bind to any infant D+ cells that are present.

○      After washing to remove unbound anti-D, add indicator red cells. Indicator cells are ficin-treated R2R2 cells that will bind to the antibody-coated infant RBCs causing agglutination (“rosettes”) that can be detected microscopically.

○      A specified number of agglutinates (eg, 3 or more in 10 fields or 7 or more in 5 fields) is designated a positive and suggests a significant FMH (>30 mL) requiring more RhIG.

When is the rosette test not valid?

●      This test is not valid if

○      the mother is Rh Positive or weak D Positive.

○      the infant is weak D Positive.

○      the infant has a positive DAT

 

What is the sensitivity of the rosette test?

 

●      Sensitivity:

○      Sufficient to detect appr 6.25ml of RBCs or 12.5 ml of fetal whole blood

○      This means a positive result indicates a significant FMH

 

What are the false positives and false negatives of the rosette test?

 

●      Limitations:

○      False positive

■      Maternal RBC are DAT pos e.g. immune hemolytic anemia (cross-linking & agglut of mother’s antibody coated cells)

■      Incomplete washing of the cells after incubation with the anti-D reagent

■      Mom is weak D phenotype

 

○      False negative

■      Baby is weak D

■      Presence of ABO incompatibility between mom and fetus if ABO incompatible fetal RBCs are cleared before the blood sample is collected for testing

■      Evaluating the possibility of FMH in conditions other than a D-negative mom and D-positive fetus

Kleihauer-Betke test

What type of test is the Kleihauer-Betke test?

 

Quantitative test

●      Kleihauer-Betke = semi-quantitative - detect cells containing Hb F (sensitivity 0.5% fetal cells)

 

What are some limitations of the KB test?

○      Has a high CV

■      Has assumptions:

■      Maternal Hct, Newborn Hct

■      Maternal blood volume

 

What is the principle of the KB test?

 

●      From SPH SOP

●      Principle:

○      Identification of F cells depends on the fact that HbF resists acid elution to a greater extent than HbA.

○      F cells take a dark stain while A cells appear as ghost cells.

■      Some reticulocytes resist acid-elution

■      Elution is carried at PH 1.5

 

What tube is used for the KB test?

 

●      Tubes: EDTA whole blood

 

What are the steps of the KB test?

●      Steps:

○      Requires positive control: washed O cord blood from blood bank (one drop) + 5 drops normal adult whole blood

○      Negative control: normal adult whole blood

○      Make 3 slides: patient, +ve and -ve control

○      Mix with blood with NaCL

○      Prepare slide… air dry…. Fix in fetal cell fixing solution….rinse with distilled water….dry...buffer..rinse….stain (erythrosin B, fast green)

 

How to calculate fetal blood loss?

 

·       PFB is the percentage of fetal blood lost;

·       FC is the observed number of fetal red blood cells;

·       MC is the observed number of maternal red blood cells (N.B. we have that

·       MC=TC-FC, where

·       TC is the total observed number of red blood cells, both maternal and fetal);

·       FW is the stillbirth weight of the fetus in kilograms

 

 

How to calculate the number of RhD vials?

An estimate of the required number of Rho(D) immune globulin vials may assume the following equations:

 

 

 

Combining those two equations results in:

 

 

This is approximately equal to:

 

Number of vials = % Fetal Cells x 1.7

Practically, if the number to the right of the decimal point is ≥5, it is rounded up to add one vial.

Example 1:  If 2.9% of fetal cells are reported on KB, what dose of RhIG would be required?

·        Volume of fetal blood:  2.9 x 50 = 145 mL

·        Number of vials = 145 mL/30 = 4.83

·        The decimal is greater than 5, therefore round up and add 1 vial (5+1).

·        Answer: 6 vials

Example 2:  If 2.6% of fetal cells are reported on KB, what dose of RhIG would be required?

·        Volume of fetal blood: 2.6% x 50 = 130 mL

·        Number of vials = 130 mL/30 = 4.33

·        The decimal is less than 5, therefore round down and add 1 vial (4+1).

·        Answer: 5 vials

 

What is the sensitivity of the KB test?

 

●      Sensitivity:

○      Count at least 2000 RBC → achieve analytic sensitivity of 0.6%

○      At this level able to detect FMH of 15 mL RBCs or 30 mL of whole blood

 

What are the limitations of the KB test?

 

●      Limitations:

○      Degree of elution of adult Hb varies from:

■      Patient to patient

■      Test run to test run

○      Test has a high CV with interobserver variation

○      Difficulty differentiating fetal Hb from adult F-cells under the microscope

 

What are some conditions with increase in F-cells in maternal circulation?

 

●      Hemoglobinopathies

○      HPFH (Hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin), sickle cell disease esp on hydroxyurea therapy

●      Thalassemia

●      Pregnancy

●      Erythropoietic stress

●      Bone marrow failure

 

 

Flow cytometry for FMH

What is the advantage of flow cytometry for FMH?

 

-        Less subjective, more precise

 

What is the sensitivity of flow cytometry for FMH?

 

●      Flow cytometry - sensitivity is 0.1%

○      Less subjective, more precise

 

What is the recommended reference method to confirm the volume of FMH (BCSH 2009)?

 

●      Flow cytometry

 

What markers do you use for Flow FMH?

 

●      Can use anti-D, anti-F

 

What are the limitations of flow for FMH?

 

●      Limitations:

○      Expensive

○      Technical expertise

○      Not 24/7

○      Inaccurate estimation of FMH if

■      Agglutinated RBCs– rack the tube to disaggregate

■      Hemolysis

○      Don’t dilute the anti-HbF reagent

■      Causes reduced fluorescence of fetal RBCs, so they are indistinguishable from maternal F cells

 

 

What do you do when a woman has a positive antibody screen?

 

●      What is the antibody?

○      Is it clinically significant

○      Is it expressed on fetal cells

●      Antibody Titre

○      Semi-quantitative - screening test

○      Not a direct predictor of HDFN

○      Critical Titre

■      Lab should probe this in which no perinatal deaths have occurred from EBF

■      When reached, need MFM

■      Usually >16 for any antibodies except for KELL!

■      Should be done with same reagents in same lab

■      This is a SALINE IAT test, 60 min incubation

■      Should not have any enhancement media or enzyme etc. for enhancement

■      Should be done Tube testing

■      Gel is higher titre

■      Cell selection should be heterozygous (other sources said homozygous however BCCH SOP said heterozygous)

■      Rising Titre

■      2 tube increase or critical titre

■      In previous affected pregnancy, clinical monitoring is initiated immediately!!

 

What is the definition of the antibody titre for HDFN?

 

●      Titre = last dilution with agglutination (macroscopically!)

○      Titre of 32 means that 32 did agglutinate, but 64 didn’t!

 

What is reported if an antibody is found in pregnancy?

 

●      Reporting the antibody

○      Clinically significant

■      Specific antibody

■      Clinical significance

■      Report antibody titre

■      Recommend follow up testing or referral

■      Request paternal sample

○      Clinically Insignificant

■      Then this is reported

●      Next steps

○      MCA doppler testing

■      Correlates with anemia

○      Cordocentesis if indicated based on MCA

■      IUT sampling with transfusion

 

Name some calculations used for RhIg dosing?

 

●      Kleihauer

●      Mollison

●      Creasy (AABB manual)

●      Foley

●      Cunningham

 

 

HDFN Clinical side of things

 

What are 5 diseases due to placental transfer of pathogenic IgG?

 

  1. HDFN
  2. FNAIT
  3. Congenital Heart Block - Anti SSA, Anti-SSB
  4. Gestational Alloimmune liver disease
  5. Maternal Grave’s disease

What are the most likely antigens to require IUTs (Netherlands)?

●      Anti-D - 75%

●      Kell - 16%

●      Other - 8%

○      c, E, e, Fya, Jka

●      NOTE: This is pre-natal/fetal disease

○      ABO is more common in the neonatal period

 

What is the incidence of Anti D formation in mom if no RhIg? How does the incidence change with a single post-partum dose? With the addition of both 28 week and post-partum dose?

12-16% Anti-D formation (some in first preg, some in subsequent)

-        Reduction to 1% Anti D with post-partum dose

-        Further reduction to 0.1% with 28-week dose

 

What are the goals If alloimmunization happens?

 

●      To prevent severe anemia causing hydrops and/or death

○      Mild anemia is well tolerated

●      To prolong pregnancy to term

○      Reduce complications of pre-term

●      To minimize morbidity from procedures

 

What is the routine management for maternal alloantibodies?

 

●      G&S at 1st prenatal visit

○      CBS does antibody screen and recommends MFM or follow up

■      Repeat G&S q4 weeks until 28 weeks, and then q2 weeks

 

Who gets referred to MFM?

●      If critical titre or Kell

○      Referral to MFM

■      MFM History:

■      Which antibody, titre

■      How was mom sensitized

■      Father of current pregnancies

■      blood type if paternity is certain

■      Previous affected pregnancies and outcome

■      Gestational age

■      Earlier onset with subsequent pregnancies!

■      Treatment required (antenatal or postnatal)

 

When do we start monitoring for Fetal Anemia?

 

■      Fetal anemia monitoring once critical titre or Kell

■      MCA doppler

■      Anemic blood will flow faster

■      Note: Gold standard is fetal cord sampling (we don’t do this!)

■      alternative is Amniotic fluid bilirubin level (Liley)

 

Fetal Genotyping

●      Amniocentesis > 15 weeks (history)

○      Risk 1:200 pregnancy loss with one procedure

●      Maternal plasma cell-free fetal DNA

○      Used if dad is heterozygous!

○      Anti-D, Anti-C, anti-c, Anti-E at >16 weeks

○      Anti-K at >28 weeks

○      Until these times, still want to do the routine management

○      Sensitivity/Specificity is approaching 100%

 

What is the purpose of the MCA doppler?

 

●      Peak velocity increases with increased cardiac output and decreased blood viscosity

●      Both Absolute value and trend are important

●      Sensitivity of 88%, but there are some misses

○      Usually over-call anemia

●      Advantage is also for Kell

 

What is the goal of the IUT Procedure?

●      Goal: Prolong to gestation close to term

○      Reduce complications of prematurity

○      Increase liver maturity to manage neonatal Hyperbili

 

What is the IUT target Hct and Access point?

●      Target is 35-45% Hct depending on Gestation age

○      Max is 50% fetal blood volume (less if hydropic)

●      Generally done >18 weeks and <35 weeks

●      Target:

○      Intrahepatic UV

○      Anterior placenta cord insertion

○      Intraperitoneal (rare)

 

What are the requirements for blood for IUT?

●      O neg (or group specific if known)

●      Negative for any antigen of Maternal Alloantibody

●      CMV negative

●      Irradiated

●      Hb S negative

●      Fresh <5-7 days

●      High Hct (0.7-0.9)

●      Washed

 

5.FNAIT

Definition of FNAIT

 

·       Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (FNAIT) is an immune-mediated cause of thrombocytopenia in neonates due to maternal anti-human platelet antigen (HPA) antibodies, most commonly anti-HPA-1a.

 

What is the definition of neonatal thrombocytopenia?

 

·       Thrombocytopenia in a neonate is defined as a platelet count of less than 150 x 109/l and is considered severe if the platelet count falls below 50 x 109/l.

 

What are the most common antibodies and their frequencies in FNAIT based on HPA types?

 

·        Anti-HPA-1a: ~80% of cases in Caucasians

·        Anti-HPA-5b: ~10-15% of cases

·        In Asian populations:

·       Anti-HPA-5b is the most common cause.

·       4a is second

     Most common case scenario: mum is HPA-1b/1b homozygous (2%) of population, dad is HPA-1a (98% of population, hetero a/b or homo a/a); baby inherited HPA-a1 from dad and mum is exposed and developed anti-PLT alloab; allo ab is IgG-> cross the placenta to bind to fetal PLTs and destroy.

 

What is the pathophysiological mechanism of FNAIT?

 

·        Maternal alloimmunization:

o   Mother forms antibodies (IgG) against paternally inherited fetal HPA (Human Platelet Antigens).

·        Placental transfer:

o   These IgG antibodies cross the placenta and enter fetal circulation.

·        Platelet destruction

·        Megakaryocyte suppression

·        Endothelial damage

 

What is the significance of the HLA-DRB3*01:01 allele in FNAIT?

 

·        HLA-DRB3*01:01 is associated with an increased risk of anti-HPA antibody formation in mothers.

·        Women with this allele are more likely to develop anti-HPA-1a antibodies, which can lead to severe thrombocytopenia in the fetus.

 

Diagnostic testing for FNAIT (3 steps)?

 

·       Maternal anti-HPA antibody screening and identification

·       HPA genotyping of mother, father and/or neonate

·       Confirmation of antibody specificity and reactivity with the monoclonal antibody immobilization of platelet antigens (MAIPA) assay

 

Complications of FNAIT (2)

 

·       ICH

·       Miscarriage

 

What are the antenatal and postnatal management strategies for FNAIT?

 

·        Antenatal Treatment:

o   No routine screening for anti-HPA antibodies in pregnant women.

o   IVIg is first-line treatment, starting at 12–16 weeks in high-risk cases (weekly).

o   Intrauterine platelet transfusion is rarely used due to high risk of complications.

o   Corticosteroids may be added, though evidence is weak.

·        Postnatal Treatment:

o   Immediate platelet transfusion to maintain platelet count >30 x 10^9/L.

o   For severe bleeding, raise platelet count to >50 x 10^9/L for at least 7 days.

o   HPA-matched platelets are preferred but unmatched units can be used if matched are unavailable.

o   IVIg and corticosteroids may be considered postnatally, but evidence is insufficient.

Kidney transplantation (6 percent)

Myasthenia gravis (5 percent)

What are the two RBC Bag types, and what are the differences?

●      B1 - Buffy coat - Top/bottom WB system

○      Used to make RBCs, plasma, platelets

○      From time the whole blood is collected, allowed to rest for at least 8 hours, and at least 3 of these on a cooling tray

○      Separation must be completed within 24 hours of collection

■      Centrifuge, and then squeeze out RBCs at bottom, plasma at top

■      Left over is buffy coat platelets

■      Note: Plasma from B1 bag is not filtered

●      B2 - Whole blood filtration system

○      Used to make RBCs and plasma, or RBCs and cryoprecipitate

■      Cannot make platelets

○      B2 bag is filtered whole blood

○      72 hours to complete production

○      24 hours is desired for cryoprecipitate production

 

What is in a unit of RBCs?

 

●      Volume: 240-340 mL (avg 290mL)

○      Anticoagulant: 110mL

■      70 mL CPD

■      110 mL SAGM

○      Plasma: <30mL (usually 10-15mL)

●      Stored in DEHP bag

 

What is the Hct of an RBC bag? How much Iron? How many Leukocytes?

 

●      Hct: 0.5-0.7 in 90%

●      Iron: 150-200mg (0.8 mg/mL)

●      Leukocytes: <5 x 10 ^6 WBC/ unit


What is the anticoagulant and Additive Solutions in RBC?

 

●      CPD: Citrate, Phosphate, Dextrose

○      21 days storage

●      CPDA-1: Citrate, Phosphate, Dextrose, Adenine

○      35 days

●      CPD SAGM: Citrate, Phosphate, Dextrose, Saline, Adenine, Glucose, Mannitol

○      42 days

 

What is the purpose of the various additive solutions in an RBC bag?

 

●      Citrate - chelates Ca2+ (anticoagulant)

●      Phosphate - Buffer to slow the acidosis

○      Diminishes loss of 2,3 DPG

●      Dextrose/Glucose - Substrate in glycolysis

●      Adenine - maintenance of ATP

●      Mannitol - protection from hemolysis

 

What are the benefits of leukoreduction?

 

●      All products are leukocyte reduced

●      Reduces FNHTR

●      Reduces CMV transmission

●      Reduces HLA- alloimmunization

●      Reduced TA-GVHD

 

If there is a RBC additive

 

-        75% have to be alive at 24 hours

How assays are used in monitoring the products

Assays:

  1. Standard aPTT-Based Clotting Assay:
    • Used for most clotting factors, including Factor VIII (e.g., Kovaltry®, Xyntha®, Advate®) and Factor IX (e.g., BeneFIX®, Rixubis®).
    • Measures clotting time to monitor the activity of infused clotting factors.
  2. Chromogenic Assay:
    • Provides more accurate activity readings for certain modified products, especially PEGylated FVIII/FIX (e.g., Adynovate®, Jivi™, Esperoct®).
    • Preferred for glyco-PEGylated products.
  3. Clot Solubility Assay:
    • Used for Factor XIII (e.g., Tretten®, Corifact®) to detect severe deficiencies by testing clot stability.
  4. Ristocetin Cofactor Assay (VWF):
    • Specifically measures the activity of von Willebrand Factor (e.g., Humate-P®, Wilate®, Vonvendi®) by assessing platelet adhesion ability.
  5. Specialized Activity/Antigen Assays:
    • Applied to proteins like Antithrombin III (Antithrombin III NF®), Protein C (Ceprotin®), and C1-Inhibitor (Berinert®, CINRYZE®, HAEGARDATM®).
  6. One-Stage Clotting Assay:
    • Commonly used for Factor VIII and Factor IX levels. Requires specific reagents for PEGylated or fusion proteins (e.g., Esperoct®, Idelvion®).

 

8.Hemophilia, diagnosis, types, medications, dosing, monitoring

 

Hemophilia A: What is the inheritance? Where is the gene located? What is the most common mutation?

 

●      X-linked recessive

●      FVIII

○      Inversion mutation of intron 22 region in 45%

●      Factor VIII located on X chromosome close to centromere

■      Huge Gene 185,000 bp, 26 exons, 25 introns

■      Intron 22 contains another Gene A of unknown function

■      2 more copies of gene A are found close to the telomere

●      50% of Hemophilia A is result of the following:

○      Genetic recombination between identical Gene A sequences

○      Resulting in rearrangement of the factor VIII gene

○      No functional factor VIII is produced

○      Can be picked up by PCR

○     

●      50% are point mutations, deletions, insertions

 

What is the half-life of Factor VIII

 

●      Half life: 8-12 hours

 

What is the recovery of factor VIII concentrate (ie. How much does 1U/kg raise the factor VIII level by?  What is the dosing schedule for major bleeding?

 

●      Recovery: 1U/kg raises plasma factor by 2%

●      Dosing:

○      Loading dose

■      40-50 U/kg for a major bleed to raise a severe factor VIII to 50-100%

○      Followed by maintenance 50% of loading dose q12

 

What are the genetics of Hemophilia B?

 

-        X-linked

-        Most 2ndary to point mutations, deletions, insertions

 

What is the recovery of factor IX concentrate (ie. How much does 1U/kg raise the factor VIII level by?  What is the dosing schedule for major bleeding?

●      FIX

○      Half life: 18-24 hours

○      Recovery: 1U/kg raises FIX by 0.8%

 

What are the severities of hemophilia and the factor levels? What type of bleeding phenotype do they have for each?

 

What are the Principles of Care for Hemophilia with bleeding?

●      Prevent and treat bleeding with the deficient clotting factor within 2 hours of symptoms!

○      Prophylactic factor replacement can be used for prevention (see below)

●      Specific factor deficiency should be treated with specific factor concentrate (whenever possible)

●      Manage in comprehensive care setting (multidisciplinary team) - yearly

○      Priorities for:

■      Bleeding prevention

■      Training/supervision of clotting factor infusions

■      Prompt bleeding management

■      Management of bleeding complications

■      Joint/muscle damage

■      Inhibitor development

■      Viral infections transmitted through products

■      Psychosocial health

○      Team members: Physician, nurse, MSK expert (PT), Lab, Social worker/Psychologist

■      Access to other specialists: Chronic pain, dentist, geneticist, herpetologist, ID, Immunologist, OBS GYN

●      Patients recognize early signs of bleeding “aura"

 

What is important information on “Factor First” cards?

 

●      ALL patients carry ID (FACTOR FIRST CARD)

○      Diagnosis

■      Baseline factor activity

■      1 stage, chromogenic

○      Severity

■      Major vs. minor

○      Inhibitor status

○      Type of product used

○      Initial dosage for

■      Severe bleeding

■      Moderate bleeding

■      Mild bleeding

■      Contact information for treating physician/clinic

○      Half-life of product

 

 

What are the different types of prophylactic Factor Replacement Therapy?

 

Treatment of Hemophilia in PREGNANCY?

 

●      Referral from medical genetics

●      30% with severe hemophilia A have no family history

●      Safe delivery

○      No vacuum, no forceps, no scalp monitor

○      Elective c-section if any issues/ emergent if complications

●      Cord blood collection

○      PTT, FVIII, FIX, genotyping

 

When do you start prophylaxis for Hemophilia?

 

TODDLER

 

●      Start prophylaxis for severe patients

○      1-3 joint bleed stage in severe/moderate

○      Usually 1 year

●      Venous access challenges: VAD may need to be placed

●      Intensive teaching for families

 

 

What are the rates of inhibitor development in hemophilia (severe vs. Non-severe?) And when do you usually get inhibitors?

 

○      Severe: 20-25%

■      Seen within 1st 30-50 exposure days

○      Non-severe: 3-13%

■      Continues to increase throughout life

 

What mutations have higher rates of inhibitors?

 

●      Certain mutations have higher rate of inhibitor:

○      Severe Hemophilia:

■      Large deletions

■      Nonsense mutations

○      Mild:

■      Certain Missense mutations: 42% chance of inhibitor

■      ARG2150His Missense mutation: 12% at 50 exposure days

 

What scenarios are most likely to precipitate inhibitors?

 

●      Age of first treatment

○      Try to avoid early treatment if possible, unless necessary

●      Immunological Danger signals

○      Peak treatment moments: high doses of factors

■      >250U/kg for >/= 5 days

○      Surgery/trauma

○      Bleeding

○      Infection

○      Vaccination

○      Comorbidity

○      Can have transient inhibitor in adults

●      Cross-reactivity of inhibitor to the patient’s endogenous factor VIII

○      Antibody against the FVIII recombinant product can also bind to a moderate/mild patient’s own FVIII, converting them to severe VIII deficiency

 

How do you treat Inhibitors?

 

●      Treatment:

○      Immune Tolerance Therapy

■      Can take 12-18 months

■      Should wait until BU <10 (predicts success)

■      Although, may not need to wait with more recent data, guidelines say to still wait

■      Inhibitor treatment

■      Factor replacement given for purpose of antibody reduction

■      Low dose: 50U/kg 3x weekly

■      High dose: 200U/kg daily

■      Ideally start when <10 Bethesda Units

○      Bypassing agents for tx

■      FEIBA, Niastase rVIIa

○      Note: If low titre, and not bleeding, may be able to just manage expectantly

 

 

How do you treat a patient who has an inhibitor?

 

●      Bleeding treatment:

○      Bypassing agents

■      FEIBA

■      Recombinant Factor VIIa (Niastase)

○      Porcine Factor VIII

■      Can use if ongoing bleeding with the bypassing agents, or not comfortable with the control on bypassing agents

■      Need to be able to do the porcine-specific assay

●      Re-challenge with FVIII

○      In adults, can re-check inhibitor titre, and consider giving VIII if the inhibitor spontaneously resolves on own

■      Check Anamnestic response

What are the factor 8 products available?

 

●      Regular HL: Xyntha, Kovaltry

●      Extended HL:

○      Adynovate - pegylated

○      Eloctate - Fc fusion

●      Recovery:

●      Dose frequency

○      Maintenance = 50% of loading dose q12 (occasionally q8h)

 

What are the Factor IX products available?

●      Recovery:

○      1U raises plasma FIX by 0.8%

●      Regular HL: BeneFIX

●      Extended HL:

○      Rebinyn (pegylated)

■      Not measured accurately with 1 stage

■      T1/2 = 90h

What is the issue with measuring Rebinyn (pegylated Factor IX)?

 

-        One-stage clotting assay results can be significantly affected by the type of activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)

-        Avoid the use of silica-based reagents, as some may overestimate the activity of REBINYN.

-        If monitoring of Factor IX activity is performed, use a chromogenic assay or selected one-stage clotting assay validated for use with REBINYN

-        If a validated one-stage clotting or chromogenic assay is not available
locally, then use of a reference laboratory is recommended.

 

What are the treatment doses for FVIII in Major, Minor, Hemarthrosis and Prophylaxis?

 

FVIII: 1 unit increases factor level by 2%

●      Major: 50U/kg = 100%

●      Hemarthrosis: 40U/kg = 80%

●      Minor: 30U/kg = 60%

●      Proph: 15-30 U/kg q2d

 

What are the treatment doses for FIX in Major, Minor, Hemarthrosis and Prophylaxis?

 

FIX: 1 unit increased factor level by 0.8%

●      Major: 120-135U/kg = 100%

●      Hemarthrosis: 80-120U/kg = 80%

●      Minor: 35-80U/kg = 60%

●      Proph: variable

Note: then round to nearest vial size

 

What is the “new” antibody for Hemophilia?

-        Emicizumab

 

What is the mechanism of action of Emicizumab?

 

-        Emicizumab is a bispecific monoclonal antibody

-        bridges activated factor IX and factor X 

-        replaces the function of missing activated factor VIII

-        restores hemostasis

 

 

What are the issues with Emicizumab in factor assays or Bethesda inhibitor assays?

 

-        Factor assays

-        Factor VIII requires incubation in order to activate it

-        There is more of a time-dependence in the test

-        Emicizumab is always "on", so will essentially shorten the clotting time of the tests

-        Inhibitor assays

-        When emicizumab is present, it will also give false negative bethesda assays, as the inhibitor does not interfere with Emicizumab binding to IXa and X

 

How to measure Inhibitor level, or residual VII level?

-        It seems that in the HAVEN trials (for Emicizumab), they didn't measure the drug level

-        But if you want to measure the residual factor VIII, or inhibitor level (Bethesda), you can use bovine factor IX and X in either a clot-based or chromogenic assay, as the Emicizumab will not bind to the bovine factors

10.Transfusion indications

Indications for Blood Products (Bloody Easy 5)

1. Red Blood Cells (RBCs)

  • Acute Blood Loss:
    • Maintain hemoglobin >70 g/L during active bleeding.
    • Liberal transfusion (>90 g/L) in gastrointestinal hemorrhage increases re-bleeding risk.
  • Critical Care/Coronary Care:
    • Transfuse if hemoglobin <70 g/L (restrictive strategy).
    • Post-cardiac surgery: Threshold of 75 g/L.
  • Perioperative Patients:
    • Transfuse one unit at a time.
    • Thresholds:
      • <70 g/L: Likely appropriate.
      • <50 g/L: Recommended.
    • Avoid transfusion if hemoglobin >90 g/L unless exceptional circumstances.
  • Chronic Anemia:
    • Transfuse only if alternatives fail. Monitor for iron overload (≥20 units transfused).

 

2. Platelets

  • Prophylactic Use:
    • Platelet count <10 x 10⁹/L in non-bleeding patients with hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia.
    • <20 x 10⁹/L for central venous catheter placement.
    • <50 x 10⁹/L for major surgery or high-risk procedures.
  • Active Bleeding:
    • Platelet dysfunction with marked bleeding (e.g., post-cardiopulmonary bypass).
    • Life-threatening hemorrhage in immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).
  • Contraindications:
    • Avoid in ITP without major bleeding.
    • Do not transfuse preemptively for minor procedures (e.g., paracentesis) if platelet count >20 x 10⁹/L.

Summary of "Platelet Transfusion: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the AABB"

This guideline by the AABB provides evidence-based recommendations for platelet transfusion in adult patients, focusing on balancing bleeding risk reduction with transfusion-associated risks. Key recommendations include:

  1. Hospitalized Patients with Therapy-Induced Hypoproliferative Thrombocytopenia
    • Recommendation: Prophylactic transfusion at platelet count ≤10×10⁹/L to reduce spontaneous bleeding.
    • Strength: Strong (moderate-quality evidence).
    • Dose: A single apheresis unit or equivalent; lower/higher doses offer no additional benefit.
  2. Elective Central Venous Catheter Placement
    • Recommendation: Prophylactic transfusion if platelet count <20×10⁹/L.
    • Strength: Weak (low-quality evidence).
  3. Elective Diagnostic Lumbar Puncture
    • Recommendation: Prophylactic transfusion if platelet count <50×10⁹/L.
    • Strength: Weak (very-low-quality evidence).
  4. Major Elective Nonneuraxial Surgery
    • Recommendation: Prophylactic transfusion if platelet count <50×10⁹/L.
    • Strength: Weak (very-low-quality evidence).
  5. Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass
    • Recommendation: Avoid routine prophylaxis in nonthrombocytopenic patients; consider transfusion for perioperative bleeding with thrombocytopenia/platelet dysfunction.
    • Strength: Weak (very-low-quality evidence).
  6. Intracranial Hemorrhage on Antiplatelet Therapy
    • Recommendation: No recommendation for or against transfusion due to insufficient evidence.
    • Strength: Uncertain (very-low-quality evidence).

 

ONTARIO CLINICAL PRACTICE RECOMMENDATIONS FOR USE OF PLATELET TRANSFUSION IN ADULTS AND CHILDREN AGED OVER 4 MONTHS

·        Platelet Count x109/L       Clinical Indication*

·        < 10 Hypo-proliferative thrombocytopenia without bleeding

·        < 20 Minor procedure not associated with significant bleeding

·        < 30 Minor (Grade 2) bleeding; anticoagulation that cannot be stopped

·        < 50 Significant bleeding (Grade 3-4); major non-neuraxial surgery; major trauma; liver biopsy; lumbar puncture

·        < 80 Epidural anesthesia

·        < 100 Central nervous system bleeding; head trauma; neuraxial surgery; ocular surgery (excluding cataract)

·        Any Platelet dysfunction with significant bleeding post cardiopulmonary bypass

·        *References to literature supporting these recommendations are provided in Appendix A.

Platelet Transfusion Not Useful or Not Appropriate

·        Platelet count greater than10x109/L, non-bleeding hypo-proliferative thrombocytopenia

·        Platelet counts above thresholds in circumstances defined above

·        Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura in absence of life-threatening bleeding

·        Platelet transfusion for the sole purpose of meeting eligibility criteria for a clinical trial*

ONTARIO CLINICAL PRACTICE RECOMMENDATIONS FOR THE USE OF PLATELET TRANSFUSION IN NEONATES AND CHILDREN UP TO AGE 4 MONTHS

·        Platelet Count x109/L Clinical Indication*

·        < 25 Stable, non-bleeding

·        < 30 Neonatal Allo-immune Thrombocytopenia (NAIT) without severe bleeding**

·        < 50 Bleeding; non-neuraxial surgery/coagulopathy

·        <50 (raise to 100, maintain >50) Neonatal Allo-immune Thrombocytopenia with intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) and/or previously affected sibling with ICH and/or previously affected sibling with ICH

·        <100 Major bleeding; major neuraxial or ocular surgery

Platelet Transfusion Not Useful or Not Appropriate

·        Platelet count above 25x109/L in stable non-bleeding neonate

·        Platelet counts above thresholds in circumstances defined above

Procedure/Context

Common Thresholds

Epidural/Spinal Anesthesia

>80,000 – 100,000/μL

·        >50,000/μL is often used for lumbar punctures and spinals.

 

3. Frozen Plasma (FFP/FP)

  • Bleeding or Invasive Procedures:
    • INR ≥1.8 due to multiple factor deficiencies (e.g., liver disease).
    • Massive transfusion with unavailable lab results.
  • Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP): First-line therapy.
  • Contraindications:
    • Mild INR elevation (<1.8).
    • Warfarin reversal (use vitamin K or PCC instead).

 

4.     Prothrombin Complex Concentrates (PCC)

·       Either 3-factor PCC, such as factors II, IX, and X, or 4-factor PCC, such as factors II, VII, IX, and X.

  • Warfarin Reversal:
    • Life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery.
    • Dosing based on INR:
      • INR <3: 1,000 IU.
      • INR 3–5: 2,000 IU.
      • INR >5: 3,000 IU.
  • Direct Oral Anticoagulant (DOAC) Reversal:
    • 2,000 IU for anti-Xa inhibitors (e.g., rivaroxaban).

 

5. Fibrinogen Concentrate

  • Bleeding with Hypofibrinogenemia:
    • Fibrinogen <1.5 g/L in trauma/surgery.
    • <2.0 g/L in postpartum hemorrhage or cardiac surgery.
  • Congenital Deficiencies:
    • Afibrinogenemia or hypofibrinogenemia.

 

6. Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG)

  • Immunodeficiency:
    • Documented antibody deficiency with recurrent infections.
  • Hematology:
    • ITP (refractory or life-threatening bleeding).
    • Post-transfusion purpura (PTP).
  • Neurology:
    • Guillain-Barré syndrome, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP).
  • Contraindications:
    • Do not use for recurrent infections without impaired antibody responses.

 

7. Albumin

  • Paracentesis:
    • Replace with 25% albumin if >5 L ascites drained.
  • Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis:
    • 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3.
  • Hepatorenal Syndrome:
    • Combined with vasoconstrictors (e.g., terlipressin).
  • Avoid:
    • Hypoalbuminemia without clinical indication.
    • Sepsis resuscitation (no mortality benefit).

 

8. Rh(D) Immune Globulin (RhIG)

  • Pregnancy:
    • Prophylaxis at 28 weeks and postpartum for Rh(D)-negative mothers.
    • Events causing fetal-maternal hemorrhage (e.g., amniocentesis).
  • Platelet Transfusions:
    • Rh(D)-negative females of childbearing potential receiving Rh(D)-positive platelets.

9. Special Considerations for Sickle Cell Disease

  • Indications:
    • Acute chest syndrome (exchange transfusion preferred).
    • Stroke prevention (maintain HgbS <30%).
    • Severe anemia (hemoglobin <50 g/L).
  • Avoid:
    • Transfusion to hemoglobin >100 g/L (risk of hyperviscosity).
    • Phenotype/genotype-matched RBCs required to prevent alloimmunization.

10. Irradiated Blood Components

  • Indications:
    • Immunocompromised patients (e.g., stem cell transplant, Hodgkin’s lymphoma).
    • Directed donations from family members.

 

Katerina Pavenski platelet transfusion

1. Platelet Basics

  • Manufacturing:
    • Derived from whole blood (70%) or apheresis (30%).
    • Pathogen-reduced platelets (Intercept™ system) use psoralen/UV treatment to inactivate pathogens; stored in platelet additive solution (PAS) with a 5-day shelf life.
  • Storage & Administration:
    • Stored at room temperature with agitation; shelf-life 7 days.
    • Administer 1 adult dose (1 apheresis unit or 1 buffy coat pool) over 60 minutes (max 4 hours).

2. Risks of Platelet Transfusions

  • Common:
    • Febrile non-hemolytic reactions (1 in 20), minor allergic reactions (1 in 100).
  • Serious but rare:
    • Bacterial sepsis (1 in 100,000), TRALI, hemolytic reactions.
  • HLA alloimmunization: 7% risk (leading to platelet refractoriness).

3. When to Transfuse Platelets

  • Prophylactic Transfusion:
    • Threshold ≤10×10⁹/L for hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia (e.g., post-chemotherapy).
    • Higher thresholds (e.g., ≤20×10⁹/L) for fever, bleeding, or procedures.
  • Therapeutic Transfusion:

Clinical Scenario

Trigger

Central line placement

<20×10⁹/L

Major non-neuraxial surgery

<50×10⁹/L

CNS surgery/ICH/TBI

<100×10⁹/L

Antiplatelet therapy + bleeding

1–2 adult doses (depending on drug)
  • Avoid transfusion in:
    • Thrombotic thrombocytopenias (TTP, HIT) unless life-threatening bleeding.
    • Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) without severe bleeding.

4. Special Requirements

  • ABO Compatibility:
    • Prefer ABO-identical platelets to optimize increments.
    • For minor incompatibility (e.g., Group O platelets to Group A recipient), reduce plasma volume or use PAS platelets.
  • Rh Compatibility:
    • RhD-negative females of childbearing potential receiving RhD+ platelets require RhIg prophylaxis.
  • Irradiation: Required for immunocompromised patients to prevent TA-GVHD.
  • HLA/HPA Selection: For refractory patients with alloimmunization (anti-HLA/HPA antibodies).

5. Platelet Refractoriness

  • Causes:
    • Immune (20%): Anti-HLA (80–90%) or anti-HPA (10–20%) antibodies.
    • Non-immune (80%): Sepsis, splenomegaly, drugs.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Poor 1-hour increment = immune cause.
    • Poor 24-hour increment = clinical cause.
  • Management: Use HLA/HPA-selected or crossmatched platelets.

6. Alternatives to Platelet Transfusions

  • Antifibrinolytics (tranexamic acid), DDAVP, topical hemostatics.
  • Limited evidence for efficacy in most scenarios.

7. Key Guidelines

  • ICTMG/AABB/BSH Recommendations:
    • Restrictive thresholds for prophylaxis (≤10×10⁹/L).
    • Avoid unnecessary transfusions in TTP/HIT/ITP.
    • Use leukoreduced platelets to reduce alloimmunization risk.

8. Test Your Knowledge

  • Example:
    • Q: A stable leukemia patient with platelet count 7×10⁹/L requires transfusion? Answer: Yes (threshold ≤10×10⁹/L).
    • Q: HLA-selected platelets are indicated for immune refractoriness, not non-immune causes.

What is platelet refractoriness?

●      Absolute <20-50, CCI <7.5

○      16-24 hours post transfusion=platelet survival

14.TM – Transfusion strategy – blood conservation

Intraoperative strategies to reduce red blood cell (RBC) transfusion focus on minimizing blood loss and optimizing patient tolerance to anemia. These strategies are crucial to improve patient outcomes and reduce the risks associated with transfusions, such as infections and immunologic reactions. Key approaches include:

 

1. Preoperative Preparation

   - Anemia management: Preoperatively optimize hemoglobin levels by treating anemia (e.g., with iron, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or vitamin B12).

   - Medication adjustment: Discontinue or modify medications that may increase bleeding risk, such as anticoagulants, antiplatelets, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), where appropriate.

 

 2. Intraoperative Techniques

   - Hemostatic agents: Use pharmacologic agents like tranexamic acid or ε-aminocaproic acid, which inhibit fibrinolysis and help reduce intraoperative bleeding.

   - Acute normovolemic hemodilution (ANH): Blood is removed from the patient before or during surgery and replaced with crystalloids/colloids to maintain blood volume. The patient’s own blood is reinfused afterward, reducing the need for allogeneic blood transfusions.

   - Cell salvage: Intraoperative cell salvage systems collect and process the patient’s shed blood, allowing it to be reinfused during the surgery. This is particularly useful in surgeries with high blood loss.

   - Controlled hypotension: Lowering the patient's blood pressure during surgery can reduce blood loss, although this needs to be done cautiously to avoid complications related to organ perfusion.

   - Point-of-care coagulation monitoring: Technologies like thromboelastography (TEG) or rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) can assess real-time coagulation status and guide blood product use more accurately, reducing unnecessary transfusions.

   - Surgical technique improvement: Employing meticulous surgical techniques, including minimally invasive surgery, can reduce blood loss.

   - Topical hemostatic agents: Use of fibrin sealants, gelatin sponges, or other local agents can help control bleeding in high-risk areas.

 

 3. Blood Conservation Protocols

   - Restrictive transfusion thresholds: Following evidence-based guidelines that suggest restrictive transfusion practices (e.g., transfusing only when hemoglobin falls below 7–8 g/dL in stable patients) can significantly reduce the use of blood products.

   - Temperature management: Maintaining normothermia during surgery helps preserve normal coagulation and reduce blood loss. Hypothermia can impair platelet function and prolong clotting times.

 

 4. Postoperative Considerations

   - Monitoring and minimizing blood draws: Limit unnecessary blood draws postoperatively to prevent iatrogenic anemia.

   - Continuing pharmacologic agents: Use antifibrinolytics or other hemostatic drugs in the postoperative period if indicated.

 

By combining these strategies, the need for RBC transfusions can be minimized, improving outcomes and conserving blood resources.

Practice Guidelines for Perioperative Blood Management

 

1. Preoperative Strategies:

  • Patient Assessment: Identifying patients at risk for blood transfusion by reviewing medical records, conducting interviews, and ordering appropriate lab tests.
  • Treating Preoperative Anemia: Administering erythropoietin (with or without iron) or iron supplements to improve hemoglobin levels, reducing the need for transfusion.
  • Anticoagulant Management: Discontinuing or transitioning patients off anticoagulants (like warfarin or antiplatelet agents) before surgery to minimize bleeding risks.
  • Autologous Blood Donation: Patients may donate their own blood preoperatively if there's enough time for erythropoietic recovery, reducing the need for allogeneic blood.

2. Intraoperative Strategies:

  • Restrictive Transfusion Protocols: Employing protocols where transfusions are given based on clinical symptoms and hemoglobin levels (typically at a lower threshold).
  • Multimodal Protocols and Algorithms: Using predetermined bundles of interventions, including transfusion algorithms and coagulation monitoring (e.g., thromboelastography), to manage blood loss.
  • Antifibrinolytic Therapy: Administering antifibrinolytics like tranexamic acid or ε-aminocaproic acid to prevent excessive bleeding during surgery, especially in high-risk procedures like cardiac or orthopedic surgeries.
  • Acute Normovolemic Hemodilution (ANH): Blood is removed from the patient preoperatively, and the blood volume is replaced with fluids to maintain normovolemia. The removed blood is reinfused during or after surgery to reduce the need for transfusion.
  • Intraoperative Cell Salvage: Collecting and reinfusing the patient’s own blood lost during surgery to reduce the need for allogeneic transfusion.

3. Postoperative Strategies:

  • Continued Monitoring for Blood Loss: Regularly assessing the surgical site for signs of excessive bleeding and monitoring hemoglobin and coagulation profiles.
  • Use of Pharmacological Agents: Administering agents like desmopressin for platelet dysfunction or continuing antifibrinolytic therapy in the postoperative phase if required.
  • Postoperative Cell Salvage: Reinfusing collected blood during the postoperative period, particularly after major surgeries such as orthopedic procedures.

4. Treatment of Excessive Bleeding:

  • Platelet and Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) Transfusions: Administering these components based on lab tests (e.g., platelet count, INR, aPTT) in cases of excessive bleeding.
  • Cryoprecipitate and Fibrinogen Concentrate: Administered in cases of low fibrinogen levels or ongoing coagulopathy.

 

15.Transfusion camp

 

LIVER PATIENTS

·       Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis - 25% albumin 1.5 g/kg within 6 hours of diagnosis, then 1 g/kg on day 3

·       Large volume paracentesis - 25% albumin, 6-8 g for every litre removed, administer soon after procedure to avoid procedural complications (hypovolemia, hyponatremia, renal impairment)

·       Acute Onset Hepatorenal syndrome Type 1 – If eligible for liver transplant, 25% Albumin 1 g/kg on Day 1, 100-200 ml on days 2-14

 

SPECIAL POPULATIONS

·       Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome – Treatment, not prevention. 25% albumin, 50-100 g over 4 hours, q4-12 h prn

·       Plasma exchange - 5 % albumin, titrated to plasma volume removed

·       Burns > 50% TBSA – In general poor quality evidence supporting use and not routinely recommended. Historically was used if unresponsive to crystalloid, 5% albumin at 0.3-0.5 ml/kg/BSA (50-100 mL/hour).
